concerns.researcher_notes: Sheet: Capacity=3120.00 MMcf/d, no ref (MISSING_REF). Enbridge factsheet (current, ~2021 vintage, opened and read via pdftotext): 'peak day capacity: 3.09 Bcf/d' = 3,090 MMcf/d for the same 1,131-mile system — this is the strongest source available (the pipeline's own operator) but is a single source and is ~1% off the sheet's figure, so I'm flagging rather than silently confirming 3,120. Separately, Wikipedia's stub article gives capacity as 'about 20 billion cubic meters (bcm) of natural gas per annum' (≈ 1,933 MMcf/d) — I checked this and it disagrees with both the sheet and the Enbridge factsheet by roughly 35-38%; given Wikipedia's article is thin/unmaintained and Algonquin has gone through multiple capacity-adding expansions since (AIM ~2017 alone added ~342 MMcf/d, per P0150, plus Atlantic Bridge), I believe the Wikipedia figure is stale/pre-expansion and should not be used to corroborate either 3,090 or 3,120 — noting it here only so a reviewer doesn't independently rediscover and get confused by the same discrepancy. Recommend confirming the precise current figure via a FERC tariff Index of Customers/Statement of Operating Conditions or a dated Enbridge/Spectra 10-K before pasting either 3,090 or 3,120 with a ref.

concerns.recommendation: correct ProposalMonth from 8 (August) to 2 (February) -- Algonquin filed the AIM Project application on February 28, 2014, not in August
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records ProposalYear=2014, ProposalMonth=8. The FERC order states unambiguously, twice (para 1 and para 53): 'On February 28, 2014, Algonquin Gas Transmission, LLC (Algonquin) filed an application in Docket No. CP14-96-000 ... for authorization to construct and operate its Algonquin Incremental Market Project (AIM Project).' The year (2014) is right but the month is off by six months. I can't rule out August referring to some other August 2014 filing/notice in this docket (e.g., an August 6, 2014 draft EIS or an August 28, 2014 data request), but none of those are the 'proposal' (initial application) event, so I'm flagging it as likely wrong rather than confirmed-correct. This is a single primary source (the certificate order itself, which is the authoritative record of its own filing date) -- I did not find a second source stating the filing month explicitly (WAMC and Wikipedia don't give a filing date), but the FERC order's own docket history is about as authoritative as a date claim can get.

concerns.recommendation: Capacity=2000 MMcf/d is not corroborated by any source found; verify against a more current operator disclosure before treating it as sourced.
concerns.researcher_notes: No source I found states 2000 MMcf/d for this project. At launch (S&P Global Platts, 2017-06-12), XcL described a '1-Bcf/d dry gas header system' plus a '200 MMcf/d wet gas system' (1,200 MMcf/d combined design, with THQ Appalachia I initially committing to 600 MMcf/d dry + 200 MMcf/d wet). XcL's own current operations page (Wayback capture 2025-06-21) describes the mature system differently again: Lean (dry) System '3+ billion cubic feet of deliverability' (3,000+ MMcf/d) and Rich (wet) System '600+ MMCF/d of processing deliverability with potential to expand to 1 BCF/d.' None of these figures is 2000 MMcf/d on its own, and combining sub-systems gives either ~1,200 (2017 design) or ~3,600-4,000+ (current, if lean+rich are summed, which may not even be the right way to combine them since one is gathering deliverability and the other is processing deliverability). This is a genuine, material disagreement across two independent snapshots in time, not a corroboration -- flagging rather than proposing a replacement number, since I can't determine which (if any) figure the sheet's 2000 is derived from. Searched both citations in the harvested pool plus the operator's current site; did not find a discrete 2000 MMcf/d statement anywhere.

concerns.recommendation: Clarify this row's scope: either (a) it is Phase I only, in which case StartYear2=2021 should be removed (2021 is Phase II's completion, a separate EIA line item with its own 93 MMcf/d capacity increment and a distinct Maritimes & Northeast Canadian entry), or (b) it is meant to represent the whole Atlantic Bridge project, in which case Capacity should be the project total (132,700 Dth/d = 132.7 MMcf/d, not the Phase-I-only 40 MMcf/d) and Length/Diameter should reflect the project's actual built pipe (6.3 mi / 42 in, which EIA books to Phase II, not Phase I). Check whether a separate 'Phase II' PID exists elsewhere in the full GEM tracker outside this batch's 46-row roster -- if not, this may be an unrecorded gap (93 MMcf/d of capacity + the Canadian Maritimes & Northeast leg have no row at all).
concerns.researcher_notes: The row currently mixes two different granularities: SegmentName='Phase I' and Capacity=40.00 MMcf/d are Phase-I-specific values (both confirmed against EIA + Enbridge + Kallanish, see the 'none' validity entry above), but StartYear2=2021 is Phase II's completion year, not Phase I's. Per EIA's historical workbook, 'Atlantic Bridge project Phase 1' (Algonquin, Completed Date 2017-11-01, Capacity 40 MMcf/d, Miles 0) and 'Atlantic Bridge Project Phase 2' (Algonquin, Completed Date 2021-01-25, Capacity 93 MMcf/d, Miles 6.3, Diameter 42in, Cost $451.8M) plus 'Atlantic Bridge Project Phase 2 (CAN)' (Maritimes & Northeast, Completed 2021-01-25, Capacity 93 MMcf/d) are THREE separate line items, not one. Enbridge's own project page corroborates: Phase I in service Nov. 2017 at 40,000 Dth/d, 'full service' only reached Jan. 2021 after the Weymouth compressor was finished. So a 'Phase I' row correctly carries Capacity=40/StartYear1=2017, but StartYear2=2021 belongs to a DIFFERENT phase with its own capacity (93 MMcf/d) that is not recorded anywhere on this row, nor (as far as this 46-row Appalachian/Mid-Atlantic roster shows) on any other row in scope -- the roster has no second Atlantic Bridge PID. This is a genuine spec/classification ambiguity, not a fabricated value, so I am not proposing a specific replacement StartYear2 -- the fix depends on a scope decision (split vs. merge) that should be made by whoever owns the row taxonomy, not inferred by this pass. I did NOT find a second, independent-of-Enbridge/EIA source that resolves this specific segment-vs-total ambiguity, since it is an artifact of how GEM structured the row, not a factual dispute between outside sources.

concerns.recommendation: update LengthKnown to 18768.00 (km) per TC Energy's current operator page, or at minimum flag the value as stale
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM currently records LengthKnown=19312.00 km. I found the EXACT origin of this number: TransCanada's own Columbia Gas Transmission page, archived by the Wayback Machine on 2018-12-13, states verbatim '12,000 mile (19,312 km) pipeline network' AND 'Transports an average of three billion cubic feet of natural gas per day' (= 3,000 MMcf/d, matching GEM's Capacity value exactly too). So the sheet's existing Length AND Capacity values are real, accurately-sourced 2018-vintage TransCanada figures — not fabricated. However, TC Energy's CURRENT live operator page (fetched 2026-09-08) states the network is now '11,899 miles (18,768 km)' — a ~2.9% reduction (101 mi / 544 km) from the 2018 figure, and no longer restates the 3 Bcf/d capacity figure at all. This is a material, sourced disagreement between the current authoritative primary source and the sheet's current value, so I am not silently passing it. Only one origin (TC Energy/TransCanada, at two points in time) is speaking to the exact figure — I searched for an independent second source (EIA pipeline pages: root 403-blocked to scripted clients; FERC Form No. 2 annual system-mileage filing: a full docket search was out of scope for a single-row pass; Wikipedia stub: no length stated) but did not find one, so tier is medium rather than high despite the strong single-source evidence.

concerns.recommendation: re-verify StartYear1=1996 against a FERC Form 2 filing or a documented company history; I could not corroborate it and general history suggests the underlying Appalachian system predates 1996 by decades
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records StartYear1=1996 for this network row with no ref. I could not find any source — TC Energy's current page, the 2018 Wayback-archived TransCanada page, the Wikipedia stub, USA Today's 2016 acquisition coverage — that states or corroborates 1996 as an in-service/start year for Columbia Gas Transmission. Columbia Gas Transmission's predecessor entities (part of the historic Columbia Gas System) operated Appalachian transmission pipe many decades before 1996; 1996 more plausibly corresponds to Columbia Gas System's emergence from Chapter 11 bankruptcy (filed 1991) around the mid-1990s, i.e. a corporate-reorganization date rather than a pipeline in-service date — but I do not have a verified citable source for that either, so I am not proposing a replacement value, only flagging the existing one as unconfirmed. A FERC Form 2 filing or a dedicated company-history page (attempted a tcenergy.com/about/history/ guess — 404) would be the next step.

concerns.recommendation: verify StartYear1 against a FERC in-service filing or PHMSA record; current 1995 may be a year late
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's StartYear1=1995 (unsourced, MISSING_REF) is in tension with the contemporary primary account. The 1993 NWI Times article (see above; hand-decoded, live, names the pipeline) lays out the conversion in two phases: Phase 1 (140 mi within Indiana) 'will begin Tuesday' (the article ran Sep 3, 1993) and 'By Nov. 1 it will be helping [NIPSCO] supply gas' -- i.e. Phase 1 targeted for the 1993-94 winter heating season. Phase 2 (the remaining 62 mi in Ohio) 'will begin in the first quarter of 1994; it will be completed by the 1994 winter heating season' -- i.e. full completion targeted for roughly Oct/Nov 1994, not 1995. gem.wiki (read for leads only, not cited) states 1995, which is presumably where the sheet's value originated, but that is a retrospective claim with no citation of its own on the wiki page for that specific year. I could not resolve the ~1-year gap with a second source in the time available: FERC eLibrary's docket search does not respond to a scripted GET (JS app), the EIA 1998 report link that might carry an as-built in-service date is blocked by a Cloudflare challenge, and naturalgasintel.com's 1998 sign-up article 404s. Flagging as a spec concern rather than silently accepting 1995: the 1994-completion account is contemporaneous trade/local reporting (arguably more reliable on execution timing than a source-less retrospective wiki claim), but 'winter heating season' language could plausibly stretch into early 1995, so this is not a slam-dunk -- recommend Baird or a follow-up pull the FERC docket (this is FERC-jurisdictional per TC Energy) for the actual in-service order/certificate date before changing the cell.

concerns.recommendation: no confident replacement value found -- flag LengthKnown=732 km (~454.8 mi) for human review rather than staging a ref or a correction
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records LengthKnown=732.00, LengthKnownUnits=km (note: this batch's own BRIEF.md paraphrases this row as '732 mi', but the worklist's actual value_cols confirm the stored unit is km -- flagging this unit-label mismatch between the brief's shorthand and the sheet's actual data for a human to double check against the live sheet). Tested hard per the batch brief's explicit instruction. Every current-day company source describes Eastern Shore's TOTAL, present-day system (which now includes P2003's 2017 Expansion and P6003's Del-Mar Energy Pathway, plus several untracked expansions -- see cross_row_leads) as either 517 miles (chpk.com, verified) or 532 miles (esng.com/about/our-pipeline-assets/, verified) -- these are SYSTEM-WIDE current totals, not valid refs for a single original-construction segment (aggregate-vs-segment rule). Arithmetic check: 517 mi (current total) - ~40 mi (P2003) - ~20 mi (P6003) = ~457 mi, which is close to but not an exact documented match for 732 km (=454.8 mi) -- suggestive but not a citable equivalence, since it ignores the many OTHER untracked expansions documented on ESNG's own history page and in Federal Register filings (1965 Bridgeville-Cambridge 30 mi, 1981 Dover-Canterbury 8 mi, 2000 Harrington-Milford 8 mi, two multi-year 2000s expansions totaling ~65 mi, 2013 White Oak Lateral 5.5 mi, 2016 White Oak Mainline Expansion, 2023 Worcester Resiliency Upgrade -- none of which are separately tracked as their own GEM rows). Summing ESNG's own history-page mileage additions against a plausible ~1959 starting mileage does not cleanly converge on 454.8 mi either. No single source -- FERC docket, EIA, trade press, or ESNG's own material -- was found stating a distinct '732 km' or '~455 mi' milestone figure for any specific year or construction phase. Concluding this is a genuine, unresolved spec discrepancy rather than staging a fabricated correction or a system-total ref that would violate the aggregate-vs-segment rule. Tier: low/unconfirmed.

concerns.recommendation: no confident replacement value found -- flag Capacity=100 MMcf/d for human review
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records Capacity=100.00 MMcf/d. Current company sources describe the SYSTEM-WIDE design deliverability as approximately 300,000 dekatherms/day (esng.com/about/our-pipeline-assets/, verified: 'designed to deliver approximately 300,000 dekatherms per day') or 294,919 dekatherms/day (chpk.com, verified) -- both are aggregate, present-day, whole-system figures reflecting decades of subsequent expansion (P2003, P6003, and the untracked expansions listed above), not a valid ref for the original 1959 mainline's own capacity under the aggregate-vs-segment rule. No source found states a distinct original (1959) or any other single-milestone capacity figure of 100 MMcf/d specifically. Left as an unconfirmed spec point rather than citing a system total.

concerns.recommendation: Update Capacity from 500.00 MMcf/d to approximately 1,500 MMcf/d (1.5 Bcf/d) — the sheet's current figure is roughly 3x too low for the present-day system.
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records Capacity=500.00 MMcf/d. This does not match ANY figure I could find for this system at ANY point in its history, and it is off by roughly 3x from the current, well-corroborated capacity. Independent sources: (1) TC Energy's own asset page (archived Sept 2023, the page the wiki cites): 'Capacity 1.5 Bcf/d' = 1,500 MMcf/d. (2) Northeast Gas Association (member-association fact sheet, independent of the operator): 'physical receipt capability of 1.7 Bcf/d.' (3) Rextag Corporation (independent commercial pipeline-data aggregator): 'System Capacity: 1.6 Bcf/d.' All three agree the system currently moves roughly 1.5-1.7 Bcf/d — none is anywhere near 500 MMcf/d. For completeness I also checked the ORIGINAL 1990-91 FERC certificate (Docket CP89-634-001): Iroquois was authorized to transport up to 575,900 Mcf/d (~576 MMcf/d) in Phase I, with initial actual deliveries around 423,000 Mcf/d — even that original design figure is higher than the sheet's 500, and the pipeline has since been expanded multiple times (compressor additions 1993-2010, plus the ExC project targeting Nov. 2023 in-service, permits still being finalized as of April 2025 per Pipeline & Gas Journal). There is no point in this pipeline's 30+ year history that the 500 MMcf/d figure matches cleanly; it reads as either a stale mid-life figure or a transcription error. I'm proposing 1,500 MMcf/d (TC Energy's own stated figure, cross-checked against two independent sources landing in the same 1.5-1.7 Bcf/d band) as the corrected value; note the small ~1.5-1.7 spread across sources reflects different measurement conventions (design vs. physical receipt capability) and should be resolved by whoever applies this against the live FERC tariff if greater precision is wanted.

concerns.recommendation: revise SegmentCost toward ~$1.6 billion (TC Energy's own final, project-specific, post-completion figure) rather than $1.75 billion, which is very likely the COMBINED Leach XPress + Rayne XPress cost estimate (a companion, non-roster Gulf Coast project filed and approved in the same docket family) misattributed to Leach XPress alone.
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records SegmentCost=1,750,000,000 USD. Every Leach-XPress-SPECIFIC cost figure found disagrees with this and clusters instead around $1.4-1.6B, while every ~$1.75-1.8B figure found is explicitly stated as the COMBINED Leach XPress + Rayne XPress total: (a) TC Energy's own 2018-01-02 in-service announcement (the most authoritative, final, project-specific figure, issued after completion): 'an investment of approximately US$1.6 billion' for Leach XPress alone (tcenergy.com, verified); (b) an independent engineering-firm case study (slidenine.com, verified, name_found) states Leach XPress's 'total cost of $1.6 billion' -- a second, independent origin agreeing with (a); (c) TC Energy's own 2017-01-19 construction-approval announcement gave an earlier, pre-completion estimate of 'approximately $1.4 billion' for Leach XPress; (d) by contrast, Marcellus Drilling News (2017-01, verified) headlines 'FERC Approves $1.8B Leach & Rayne XPress Pipeline Projects' and states this is the COMBINED figure for both projects together (citing an original August-2014 Columbia Pipeline Group estimate of $1.75B combined) -- i.e., $1.75B/$1.8B is a two-project total, not Leach XPress's own segment cost. Rayne XPress is a Gulf Coast Louisiana project, not one of this batch's 46 rows, so there is no sibling GEM row this total could correctly belong to either -- it simply should not be on P0209 as a stand-alone figure. Tier: high for the $1.6B correction (2 independent, Leach-specific sources: TC Energy's own completion release + an independent case study); the combined-cost hypothesis for the $1.75B origin is medium-confidence reasoning, stated as such.

concerns.recommendation: Correct Diameter to a uniform 30-inch (drop the 14 and 24); correct SegmentCost to ~$654 million (FERC-certified); Capacity is a closer call -- flag the 500 vs 525(.4) MMcf/d gap for a researcher decision rather than force it.
concerns.researcher_notes: DIAMETER: the same FERC amendment notice that pins the route (govinfo.gov FR-2006-01-19) states the built Phase I line is 'about 181.7 miles of 30-inch-diameter pipeline' -- a single, uniform diameter, no mix. Oil & Gas Journal ('182-mile ... 30-in.'), Energy Intelligence ('182 miles of 30-inch pipe'), and NiSource's 10-K ('182-mile-long, 30-inch-diameter pipeline') all independently agree: uniform 30-inch. The sheet's '24' most likely bleeds in from the ORIGINAL (never-built-as-such) 2002 project's eastern Rockland/Westchester-to-Mount Vernon leg, which WAS specified at 24-inch per the same FERC record -- i.e. the same location conflation documented in the attribution finding above, carried into the diameter field. '14' has no source anywhere I found (OGJ, Energy Intelligence, NiSource 10-K, DT Midstream, TC Energy, FERC notice, industrialinfo.com) -- it does not correspond to any known Millennium mainline, lateral, or historical-proposal diameter I could locate; flagging it as unconfirmed/likely a data-entry artifact rather than asserting a specific origin. CAPACITY: OGJ literally states 'Phase 1 designed to transport 500 MMcfd of gas' -- a direct match for the sheet's 500.00. But FERC's OWN 2006 amendment notice states the Phase I project's capacity as 'about 525,400 decatherms per day (Dth/d)' (~525 MMcf/d), and NiSource's 10-K independently states 'transport up to 525,400 Dth per day.' That's FERC's certificate figure plus one more independent corroboration vs. OGJ's single, slightly lower figure -- a real but modest (5%) disagreement. Leaving the contested candidate blank rather than forcing 525.4, since OGJ's exact match to the current sheet value is itself real evidence, not noise; a researcher should weigh FERC's certificate (525.4) against OGJ's stated 500 and decide. COST: NiSource's 10-K and the 2006 FERC notice disclose no cost figure; an earlier (2006, pre-construction) industrialinfo.com article citing FERC's initial estimate says 'over $350 million' capital cost -- clearly stale, since costs typically rise through construction. Natural Gas Intelligence's trade-press article on project completion states directly (confirmed by fetching and reading the full article text): 'FERC certified the project at a cost of $654 million.' Nothing found anywhere corroborates the sheet's $800,000,000 figure; recommend $654,000,000 sourced to NGI/FERC's certification, pending a check against the FERC certificate order itself if a researcher wants a fully primary cite.

concerns.recommendation: correct Diameter from '29, 36' to '24, 36' (and note the 0.4 mi of 30-inch replacement pipe on existing Line SM-80, if the sheet wants to capture it)
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records Diameter='29, 36' in. FERC's own certificate order (the primary, authoritative source — 161 FERC P 61,314, para. 7, docket CP16-357) states the Mountaineer XPress Project consists of THREE new/replacement pipe segments: 'approximately 164.5 miles of new 36-inch-diameter pipeline (MXP-100)'; 'approximately 6.0 miles of new 24-inch-diameter pipeline (MXP-200)' (the Sherwood Lateral in Doddridge County); and 'approximately 0.4 mile of 30-inch-diameter replacement pipeline' on the existing Line SM-80/SM-80 Loop in Cabell County. There is no 29-inch segment anywhere in the FERC order's facilities description (searched the full order text for '29-inch' and '29-inch-diameter' — zero hits). GEM's '29' most likely traces back to nsenergybusiness.com's (GlobalData) project page, which states 'a 10km segment of 29in-diameter in the Doddridge county' — this appears to be GlobalData's own transcription error (24 misread/mistyped as 29; the location — Doddridge County — and approximate length — 10km vs FERC's 6.0 mi/~9.7km — otherwise line up exactly with FERC's MXP-200 lateral), since no independent source corroborates '29-inch' and the primary regulatory filing is unambiguous. I could not find a second source that independently states '24-inch' in so many words (only the FERC order itself), but the FERC order is the controlling regulatory document and is dispositive here; nsenergybusiness's '29in' is the outlier and is not an independent corroboration of the current GEM value, it appears to be its unsourced origin. Recommend replacing '29' with '24' (candidate value '24, 36'); the 0.4 mi/30-inch replacement segment on the existing Line SM-80 is a minor abandonment-and-replace item, not new capacity-adding pipe, and may not need its own diameter entry depending on sheet convention. [QC] independent=yes claimed on 1 surviving ref(s) from 1 publisher(s) -> no; tier high -> medium (single source).

concerns.recommendation: consider updating SegmentCost from 3,030,000,000 to the better-corroborated actual final cost of ~3,200,000,000 USD (or add SegmentCostYear/context distinguishing estimate-vs-actual)
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records SegmentCost=3,030,000,000 USD with NO ref and no SegmentCostYear. Three distinct cost figures surfaced across the project's timeline, and none of them is exactly 3.03bn: (1) Columbia Gas's ORIGINAL 2016 FERC rate filing put the incremental recourse reservation charge basis on an estimated project cost of '$2.059 billion' (FERC order para. 12, CP16-357) — this matches nsenergybusiness.com's 'Estimated Investment $2bn' (an early-stage estimate, both pre-construction); (2) after 'significant cost overruns that stemmed from delays in regulatory approvals, high demand for construction resources and others,' the actual final investment reported in 2019 was '$3.2 billion' — stated independently by TWO sources: Zacks Equity Research (republished on finance.yahoo.com, 2019-03-04: 'The company invested $3.2 billion in the project ... The project was earlier expected to be completed by 2018-end, with an investment of $2.6 billion') and Alpha Three, a construction-scheduling contractor on the project ('With a project value of approximately $3.2 billion'). $3.2bn is closer to GEM's $3.03bn than the original $2.06bn estimate is, but it is not an exact match, and it is the number two independent sources converge on for the actual, as-built cost — while GEM's $3.03bn currently has no ref and no traceable source at all. Recommend citing $3.2bn (candidate 3200000000) if the sheet wants the final-actual figure, or keeping $3.03bn only if Baird can identify its original source (possibly a slightly earlier interim estimate) and pairing it with a ref; as it stands the cell is asserting a number two purpose-built research passes could not verify. Searched for a third source/primary FERC rate-case cost-of-service filing stating a single all-in final capital cost; the order itself only gives the 2016 pre-construction estimate ($2.059bn) and does not restate a final actual cost (FERC orders on cost-of-service don't require post-construction cost reconciliation to be refiled in the same docket).

concerns.recommendation: flag Capacity=1500 MMcf/d as the FERC-certificated/historical design figure; both current co-owners' own asset pages now state ~1.4 Bcf/d as the current design capacity — a genuine ~7% discrepancy worth a researcher note or a distinct current-vs-certificated capacity field, not a silent overwrite in either direction
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM's Capacity=1500 MMcf/d is well-corroborated as the ORIGINAL FERC-CERTIFICATED figure: the FERC order itself, the 2020 Federal Register notice ('the total 1,500,000 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of certificated capacity' — Dth/d and MMcf/d are treated as numerically equivalent in this docket), the Pipeline & Gas Journal Oct-2018 Ongoing Projects PDF ('Capacity: 1.5 Bcf/d'), and contemporaneous 2017 press (Detroit News: 'capable of carrying 1.5 billion cubic f[eet]'; Canton Rep: 'will carry up to 1.5 billion cubic feet') all independently agree on 1.5 Bcf/d = 1500 MMcf/d as the certificated/design capacity at construction. HOWEVER, both current co-owners' own current-day asset pages give a materially lower figure: DT Midstream's page states the system has 'current capacity of approximately 1.4 Bcf per day,' and Enbridge's own current factsheet states 'Design capacity: Up to 1.4 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d).' This is not a single-source outlier — it is the SAME lower figure independently restated by both 50/50 joint-venture partners on their own most-current asset pages, a materially different (~7%, ~100 MMcf/d) number from the certificated 1500 figure, and it postdates the certificate by several years. Plausible explanations (not resolved with material in hand): the certificated 1,500,000 Dth/d volume was never fully subscribed/utilized at 100% of nameplate (the 2020 Federal Register notice itself notes NEXUS had only 'increased firm commitments ... to more than 1,315,000 Dth/d' as of mid-2020, short of the full 1.5 Bcf/d), or the owners' marketing copy is describing subscribed/contracted-plus-headroom capacity rather than engineered/certificated capacity, or a physical derate. Recommend keeping 1500 as the certificated/historical value with a note, OR adding a distinct 'current design capacity ~1.4 Bcf/d per current owner disclosures' annotation — flagging for a researcher/Baird decision rather than silently picking one number.

concerns.recommendation: flag SegmentCost as the FERC pre-construction ESTIMATE, not the reported as-built investment; ask Baird which the field is meant to hold
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM's SegmentCost=780,000,000 USD matches the FERC certificate order EXACTLY and verbatim ('Columbia estimates the total cost of the WB XPress Project to be $780 million', para. 10, and restated at para. 622) -- so the current value is directly sourced and not fabricated. But every source describing the COMPLETED project states a different, higher figure: TC Energy's own Eastern Build and Western Build in-service announcements both say 'an approximate US$900 million investment'; Natural Gas Intelligence's independent in-service article calls it 'The $900 million WB Xpress project'; offshore-technology.com's independent profile also states 'Cost: $900 million investment'. That is three independent post-construction sources (operator, one trade-press outlet, one industry-directory profile) all agreeing on $900M against one primary regulatory source's $780M PRE-construction estimate from the Dec. 2015 application. This reads as the normal estimate-vs-actual-cost gap (FERC applications routinely under/over-shoot final cost), not an error in either figure -- but the sheet currently carries the earlier, lower estimate rather than the figure every source uses once the project is actually built. Flagging for a human call on which the SegmentCost field is meant to record (as-filed estimate vs. as-built cost) rather than silently overwriting a value that IS directly sourced.

concerns.recommendation: re-research current system Capacity before adding a ref to the Capacity cell; do not cite the RBN Energy 'Empire North Expansion' article for the Main Line's capacity
concerns.researcher_notes: The current Capacity value (300.00 MMcf/d) is unsupported as sourced and materially disputed by an independent record. Reading the gem.wiki page itself (not cited): the 'Main Line' section's ONLY footnote for 'Capacity: 300 million cubic feet per day [1]' is citation [1], which is 'Empire North Expansion, RBN Energy' -- an article about the DIFFERENT, later (2020) Empire North Expansion Project (GEM's own separate row, P2531), not about the Main Line. P2531's own recorded capacity is ALSO 300.00 MMcf/d, which is exactly the coincidence the sweep brief flagged as suspicious. concerns.recommendation: correct LengthKnown from 12 to 13 (best-supported as-built figure); note genuine 12-14 mi spread across otherwise-credible sources

concerns.recommendation: set LengthKnown=0 / LengthKnownUnits blank / Diameter blank / DiameterUnits blank -- this is a compression-only capacity expansion, not a new pipe segment; do not paste 40.2 km / 26 in
concerns.researcher_notes: The row exists and is real (FERC Docket No. CP18-89-000, 'Empire North Project'), but its recorded LengthKnown=40.20 km (25 mi) and Diameter=26.00 in do not match any physical pipe FERC or the operator describes for this project -- the project built ZERO new mainline pipe. Five independent-of-each-other documents agree on the facility list: (1) FERC's own Notice of Intent to Prepare an EA (Federal Register 2018-07924, filed/opened Feb. 16, 2018): 'The Empire North Project would consist of the following facilities: A new 21,000 horsepower (hp) compressor station in Jackson Township, Tioga County, Pennsylvania; a new 32,000 hp compressor station in the Town of Farmington, Ontario County, New York; modifications of the existing regulator valves and station piping and installation of metering facilities at the existing New Victor Regulator Station...; minor modifications to the existing Jackson Meter and Regulator Station...; and upgrading the maximum allowable operating pressure of the Empire Connector Pipeline (ECP) from 1,290 psig to 1,440 psig. The ECP is an existing 76.6-mile-long, 24-inch-diameter pipeline that runs from Victor, New York to Corning, New York' -- i.e. the only pipe named is a DIFFERENT, already-existing, already-counted (on the Main Line row, P0288) segment with a different length (76.6 mi, not 25) and different diameter (24 in, not 26), in a different state (wholly within New York, not PA-to-Ontario). Total land disturbance for the whole project is stated as 50.4 acres -- consistent with two compressor-station sites, not with 25 miles of new linear pipeline construction (which would run to hundreds of acres of temporary ROW). (2) National Fuel's own official 'Empire North Project Fact Sheet' PDF (nationalfuel.com): the facilities list is two new compressor stations + two 'minor modifications' to existing stations + an MAOP uprate on the existing ECP explicitly noted as 'not expected to require any construction-related activities' -- no pipeline mileage anywhere in the facility list. (3) National Fuel's own SEC 8-K investor-presentation exhibit (2019, EDGAR accession 0001193125-19-280494) states outright: 'No new pipeline construction' -- the company's own securities filing, under legal disclosure obligations, using that exact phrase; infrastructure is described as '2 new compressor stations in NY (1) & Pa. (1)'. (4) National Fuel's own current, FERC-effective Empire Pipeline Gas Tariff (effective Sept. 15, 2020, and still governing rates as of the version searched) defines, at Section 1.19 of its General Terms and Conditions: '"Empire North Capacity" shall mean firm transportation capacity resulting from Transporter's incremental facility expansion project authorized in Commission Docket No. CP18-89-000' -- the tariff's own vocabulary treats 'Empire North' purely as a CAPACITY product (paired with an 'Empire North Compressor Fuel Retention' percentage), never as a named physical pipeline segment, in contrast to how the same tariff names the 'Original Empire Pipeline' and the 'Empire Connector' as actual physical assets. (5) A peer deep-sweep shard on this same wiki page's other GEM row (P0288, Empire Pipeline Main Line, in this same batch) independently reached the identical conclusion from its own research and flagged it as a cross-row lead for this exact row, quoting nationalfuel.com's current 'About Empire Pipeline' page: 'In 2020 Empire placed the Empire North Project into service, which saw the construction of two new compressor stations...' with no mention of new pipe. The apparent origin of the erroneous 40.2 km/26 in figures: RBN Energy's project data card for 'Empire North Expansion' (archived, since the live page 403s bots) lists 'Diameter: 26 inches' and 'Length: 25 miles' alongside Origin: Jackson, PA and Destination: Chippawa, ON -- these numbers match the sheet's LengthKnown/Diameter EXACTLY, strongly suggesting RBN Energy's card (via gem.wiki's citation of it) is the sheet's source, and RBN's card appears to describe the general PA-to-Ontario corridor over which the new/uprated capacity flows, not the footprint of new construction. Per this sweep's own standing convention (already applied in this same batch to Rockies Express Zone 3 East-to-West, and to the len-0 Rover phases/Vector P3202): an expansion project that adds capacity via compression/reversal with no new mainline pipe gets LengthKnown=0, Diameter blank -- that convention applies squarely here. Status=operating, Fuel=Gas, StartYear1=2020, and the PA/Ontario endpoints are all independently confirmed (see fills[] below) and are NOT in question -- only the physical Length/Diameter attribution is wrong.

concerns.recommendation: verify Capacity/CapacityUnits against the original FERC certificate (docket CP15-17) -- likely a units conflation between MMcf/d and Dth/d, not just rounding

EIA's July 10, 2017 'Today in Energy' article (US government, independent of the operator) states explicitly: 'Sabal Trail Phase I is designed to have a total capacity of 810 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d)' -- a different figure, in the SAME unit GEM uses (MMcf/d), not just a unit-conversion artifact. Natural gas typically runs ~1.02-1.03 MMBtu(Dth) per Mcf, so 810 MMcf/d x ~1.025 =~ 830,000 Dth/d -- i.e. the 810-MMcf/d and 830,000-Dth/d figures plausibly describe the SAME underlying capacity in two different units (volumetric vs. energy-content), not a genuine disagreement on the physical capacity. That makes GEM's cell -- '830.00' explicitly labeled 'MMcf/d' -- look like it may have inherited the 830 figure from a Dth/d source without the unit conversion, which would overstate the true MMcf/d capacity by ~2.5%. The original 2014 FERC Notice of Intent (Federal Register, an independent regulatory source) gives yet a third, earlier planning-stage figure: 'an initial capacity of 800,000 dekatherms per day (Dth/d)'. None of the three sources found state '830 MMcf/d' outright. Flagging as a spec concern rather than silently passing -- recommend the researcher pull the actual FERC certificate order (CP15-17) or Sabal Trail's tariff for the authoritative Phase I design capacity and confirm the correct unit label.

(2) A Hart Energy article (14 Oct 2011, 'Sea Robin Pipeline Delivers Offshore Volumes To Gulf, Midwest' by Frank Nieto -- live fetch 403'd, recovered via Wayback, but only the archived page's meta/summary text survived, not the full paywalled body) states the system 'is 440 miles in length with a capacity of 1 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d)' -- length rounds fine to 438, but capacity (1.0 Bcf/d) is neither GEM's 1.26 Bcf/d nor the 10-K's 2.0 Bcf/d, a third figure. Capacity=1,260 MMcf/d has one precise, authoritative origin (the court/FERC record) but two independent later sources cite meaningfully different numbers (1,000 and 2,000 MMcf/d) spanning 13 years apart -- consistent with a pipeline whose throughput/peak-day capacity changed via looping or compression additions between 1997 and 2020 rather than with GEM simply being wrong, but I cannot rule out staleness. concerns.recommendation: flag for Baird review — do not auto-change: verify whether Capacity should be the FERC-certificated maximum (~2,125,000 Dth/d, roughly 2,050-2,125 MMcf/d) rather than the currently staged 1,900.00 MMcf/d

concerns.recommendation: verify Capacity/CapacityUnits against the actual FERC certificate/tariff for Phase II -- EIA's 170 MMcf/d and Duke's ~200,000 Dth/d do not reconcile with a simple unit-conversion factor
concerns.researcher_notes: GEM records Capacity=170.00 MMcf/d for Phase II. EIA's Aug 24, 2020 'Today in Energy' article (US government, independent of the operator) states verbatim: 'the second phases of the Sabal Trail Pipeline (0.17 Bcf/d)...entered service in April', an EXACT match to GEM's 170.00 MMcf/d. However, Duke Energy's FY2020 10-K (an independent JV-partner SEC filing, not tracing to EIA or the operator) states: 'Phase II of Sabal Trail went into service in May 2020, adding approximately 200,000 Dth of capacity to the Sabal Trail pipeline.' Natural gas typically runs ~1.02-1.035 Dth per Mcf, so 170,000 Mcf/d x ~1.03 =~ 175,000 Dth/d -- notably short of Duke's stated ~200,000 Dth, a gap of roughly 14% that ordinary volumetric-vs-energy-content unit conversion does not explain. This mirrors the SAME type of Capacity discrepancy the sibling shard P0249.json flagged for Phase I (GEM 830 MMcf/d vs EIA 810 MMcf/d) -- following that shard's precedent, flagging as a spec concern rather than silently passing. Recommend the researcher pull the actual FERC order/tariff authorizing Phase II's specific incremental capacity to resolve which figure (170 MMcf/d or a Dth-derived ~194,000-196,000 Mcf/d) is the correct certificated design capacity.

concerns.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: confirmed independently of GEM. FERC Federal Register Notice of Application, Docket No. CP05-64-000 (filed Feb. 1, 2005; published 70 FR 7724, Feb. 15, 2005) states verbatim: 'FGT proposes to construct a new 17,000 horsepower electric compressor station and approximately 1,600 feet of 18-inch mainline extension. Separately, EIA's own 'Historical Projects (1996-2024)' table (eia-naturalgaspipelineprojects.xlsx, sheet 'Historical Projects (1996-2024)') carries a discrete row: Project Name 'FGT Turkey Point Lateral', Operator 'Florida Gas Trans Co', Project Type 'Lateral', Status 'Completed', Completed Date 2006-12-01, Year In Service 2006, Beg_State/End_State FL/FL, Cost (millions) 19.6, Miles 0.3, Additional Capacity (MMcf/d) 100, Diameter (in) 24, Authority FERC, Docket Number CP05-64. GEM's Length (0.30 mi), Diameter (24 in), Capacity (100 MMcf/d) and StartYear1 (2006) all match this EIA row exactly. CAVEAT ON INDEPENDENCE: both of these sources ultimately trace to the same underlying FERC docket (CP05-64) — the EIA table's own 'Authority/Docket Number' columns cite that docket as its source, and the Federal Register notice is FERC's own restatement of the company's filed application. Per the sweep's independence rule ('FERC + the applicant's own filing IN that FERC docket are ONE origin'), this is closer to one paperwork trail reported via two federal publications than two truly independent investigations. I searched for a third, genuinely separate source — Kinder Morgan's/Energy Transfer's FGT system-map/tariff pages, PHMSA special-permit filings for FGT, the NRC Turkey Point Units 6&7 COL environmental report (which would independently describe the existing gas lateral serving the plant), and general trade press from 2005-2006 — and found none that states these specific figures; the NRC PDFs (nrc.gov/docs/ML1025/ML102580481.pdf and ML1431/ML14311A254.pdf) both 403'd to scripted fetches, and the FGT system map (fgttransfer.energytransfer.com/ipost/FGT/maps/system-map) returns 200 but is a static/interactive map with no extractable text naming the lateral. So EXISTENCE and CLASSIFICATION (it is genuinely an interstate FERC-jurisdictional lateral, not gathering/gas processing) are solid; the numeric SPEC values are corroborated but from what is effectively a single origin. NOTE ALSO: the FERC notice frames the 24-inch lateral as already 'existing' as of Feb. 2005, while the compressor-station/tee project itself (the ~1,600 ft of 18-inch mainline extension) is what completed in Dec. 2006 per EIA — so 'StartYear1 = 2006' most likely marks the in-service date of this compressor/tie-in upgrade project (which EIA books under the lateral's name), not necessarily the very first construction of the 24-inch pipe itself, which may predate 2005. This is a GEM-schema granularity issue (project vs. original construction), not an existence/duplicate problem — no other roster PID represents an earlier 'Turkey Point Lateral' segment, so there is nothing to merge or split against. CLASSIFICATION: correctly recorded as an interstate transmission lateral (NGA section 7 jurisdictional), not a gathering line. DUPLICATE: checked against all 49 other roster rows — no other PID has this length/diameter/capacity combination or documents the same Miami-Dade/Turkey Point location; not a duplicate. SegmentCost DISCREPANCY: EIA's $19.6 million does not match the sheet's $19,400,000 — close (about 1%) but not an exact match, so I am not staging it as a confirming ref; flagged above for Baird's review rather than silently passed.

concerns.researcher_notes:
EXISTENCE/CLASSIFICATION: solid. This is a real, FERC-certificated segment of the Florida Gas Transmission interstate system (Docket CP00-40), correctly classified as an operating natural-gas transmission expansion. Confirmed by: (1) FERC's own Federal Register notices for Docket CP00-40 (govinfo.gov FR-2001-07-19 / 01-18025, and federalregister.gov full-text 00-22258) describing the Phase V Expansion Project in Mississippi/Alabama/Florida; (2) two independent trade-press articles (Oil & Gas Journal 2003 'Florida Gas Transmission completes Phase V expansion, begins Phase VI'; IndustrialInfo.com 2001) describing the same project's construction and completion; (3) EIA's own 'Natural Gas Pipeline Projects: Historical Projects' table (the same source GEM's wiki page footnotes as [4]), which carries a discrete line item 'FGT Phase V Stage 4' -- Completed 2003-05-01, States MS/AL/FL, Cost $132M, Miles 136, Additional Capacity 130 MMcf/d, Diameter 24/36/16 in, Docket CP00-40 -- an EXACT match to every value on this GEM row; (4) Energy Transfer's own current (June 2026) 'FGT Phase IX' factsheet PDF, confirming FGT is still an active, operating interstate system today ('FGT is a subsidiary of Citrus LLC, a partnership between Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan. The pipeline is operated by Energy Transfer'). No hallucination/GEM-only-entity risk here.

DUPLICATE check against the roster: P4035 (Stage 4, 136mi, MS-AL-FL, completed 2003-05) is NOT the same physical facility as sibling rows P4036 ('Phase V Stage 3', 15mi, FL only, completed 2002-12) or P4037 ('Phase V Stages 1-2', 64mi, MS-AL-FL, completed 2002-04) -- EIA's Historical Projects table treats all three as separate FERC-tracked project/completion milestones under the same certificate (CP00-40), consistent with how GEM already splits other multi-phase FGT expansions (Phase VI/VII/VIII each get their own row too). Recommend no merge.

SPEC CAVEAT (why this isn't a plain pass): summed across the three Phase V stage rows, GEM/EIA give 136+15+64 = 215 miles and 130+180+298 = 608 MMcf/d of stage-level 'additional capacity'. Two independent sources describing Phase V as a WHOLE project instead report ~165.8-167 miles of new pipe (FR-2001-07-19 final EIS-availability notice: 'approximately 165.8 miles of pipeline and 125,215 HP'; OGJ 2003: '167 miles of new pipeline and 132,615 hp'; IndustrialInfo 2001: '167 miles ... $452 million') and a net 428 MMcf/d capacity increase (OGJ, IndustrialInfo, both). That is a ~30% mileage overage and a ~42% capacity overage versus the aggregate figures -- a real inconsistency, not proof Stage 4's own 136mi/130MMcfd is wrong. Two innocent explanations exist and I could not rule between them: (a) capacity additions on sequential looped segments of one system are not simply additive end-to-end (the smallest downstream link caps net throughput), which plausibly explains the capacity gap alone; (b) FGT's original Dec-1, 1999 application (federalregister.gov full-text 00-22258, footnote 1) was for 'about 215.4 miles of pipeline, 15.7 miles of rehabilitated mainline' -- almost exactly the stage-level sum -- then was amended down to 191.5mi (Aug 2000) and again to ~165.8mi by the final July 2001 certificate; EIA's per-stage entries may trace to an earlier proposal iteration rather than final as-built facilities. Cross-checked against 8 OTHER FGT sub-project rows in this same EIA table (Phase IV, VI, VII Phase 1, VIII, Turkey Point Lateral, East Leg, Alabama Power Lateral, Mobile Bay Lateral -- see cross_row_leads) and every one of those EIA figures is an EXACT match to GEM's existing sheet values, so EIA is not a generally unreliable source here -- the Phase V 3-way split is the one place in this family where the parts don't cleanly reconcile to the reported whole. Recommend pulling FERC's actual certificate order (96 FERC P61,143, issued 7/27/2001, Docket CP00-40) for its per-facility mileage table before treating either the stage split or the aggregate figures as the final word; I could not reach the order text itself (elibrary.ferc.gov requires an interactive docket search, not a static URL).

concerns.researcher_notes:
EXISTENCE/CLASSIFICATION: real and correctly classified. FGT's 'Phase V Expansion Project' is independently and repeatedly documented: FERC issued ONE certificate (Docket Nos. CP00-40-000, -001, -002) on July 27, 2001 authorizing the whole project (Federal Register FEIS notice, 66 FR ~2001-07-19, verified live at govinfo.gov: 'approximately 165.8 miles of pipeline loops and laterals,' '132,615 horsepower of additional compression at nine existing and three new compressor stations,' 'Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida,' cost '$452 million'). Two independent trade-press accounts of the COMPLETED project agree closely: Oil & Gas Journal ('166 miles of pipeline and 133,000 hp of compression,' '428 MMcfd of incremental firm gas transportation service') and IndustrialInfo.com ('167 miles of new pipeline,' 'adds 428 million cubic feet per day, bringing total system capacity to over 2.1 billion cubic feet daily,' '$452 million investment,' majority completed April 2002, construction in Mississippi/Alabama/Florida). Three independent origins (the regulator's own EIS notice, and two separately-bylined trade publications) agree Phase V as a WHOLE was ~166-168 miles / +428 MMcf/d / $452M -- built as one FERC-authorized project, not sub-certificated by 'stage.'

SPEC / DUPLICATE-ADJACENT FINDING (the reason for the caveat): GEM records this single project as THREE separate rows -- P4037 'Phase V Stages 1-2' (this row: 64 mi / 298 MMcf/d / $320M / start 2002), P4036 'Phase V Stage 3' (15 mi / 180 MMcf/d / $13M), and P4035 'Phase V Stage 4' (136 mi / 130 MMcf/d / $132M). Summed across all three: 215 miles / 608 MMcf/d / $465M -- respectively 29%, 42%, and 3% ABOVE every independently-verified total above. But the arithmetic is not random: P4037 (298 MMcf/d, $320M) + P4035 (130 MMcf/d, $132M) ALONE reproduce the independently-verified totals EXACTLY -- 298+130=428 MMcf/d (matches '428 MMcfd' / '428 million cubic feet per day' verbatim in both trade-press sources) and 320+132=$452M (matches '$452 million' verbatim in all three sources). Adding P4036 ('Stage 3': 180 MMcf/d, $13M) on top overshoots the true total by exactly P4036's own capacity and cost figures. This is strong circumstantial evidence that P4036 ('Stage 3') is either a duplicate/phantom entry or was double-counted, while THIS row's values (P4037, 298 MMcf/d / $320M) look like a genuine, correctly-allocated 2/3 share of the real project -- I just could not find any independent document that names 'Stages 1-2' specifically to confirm the 64-mile/298-MMcf/d split at that granularity (mileage alone does not reconcile as cleanly: P4037+P4035 = 200 mi vs. the ~166-168 mi independently reported, a ~33-34 mi gap even excluding P4036 -- so the length figures for these rows are not fully explained by this exercise). Per the aggregate-vs-segment rule, I did NOT cite any of these three system-level Phase V sources as a ref for this row's Length/Diameter/Capacity/Start/SegmentCost cells (none of them name 'Phase V Stages 1-2'); those cells are left UNRESOLVED with this note instead, per instructions ('note it and file a validity concern instead').

None of these sources state a single crisp founding/in-service year, so I am not fabricating a replacement value, but 1996 is affirmatively wrong -- it most likely reflects El Paso's 1996 acquisition of Tenneco (a different, though related, pipeline family) being miscoded onto this row, or a legacy GEM data-entry artifact. concerns.recommendation: Change Status from 'cancelled' to 'operating'. concerns.researcher_notes: This is the single most consequential finding on this row: a project GEM records as 'cancelled' (ShelvedYear=2018, CancelledYear=2020, ShelvedCancelledType=inferred -- i.e. nobody found a dated source for the cancellation, it was inferred from dormancy) was in fact completed, not cancelled. Timeline reconstructed from Talen's own SEC filings plus five independent, dated Marcellus Drilling News (MDN) trade-press articles: (1) June 7, 2016 -- Talen's board approves the coal-to-gas conversion project and a competitive RFP process to select a third party to build the 15-mile lateral (SEC 8-K; MDN 2016/06 article same week). (2) December 2016 -- MDN reports Talen has put the conversion 'on hold' (MDN 2016/12 article) -- this is almost certainly the event GEM's dormancy heuristic misread as a cancellation, two years before the ShelvedYear=2018 it actually recorded. (3) November 2020 -- MDN reports Talen, under Sierra Club litigation pressure, signs a pledge to convert its coal-fired plants including Montour to gas (MDN 2020/11 article) -- the project is revived, not dead. (4) February 2022 -- MDN reports Talen actively working on the Montour coal-to-gas conversion (MDN 2022/02 article). (5) August 2023 -- MDN reports the Montour PA coal-to-gas conversion is 'nearly done' (MDN 2023/08 article, title itself is the dated claim). (6) September 5, 2024 -- Talen's own SEC-filed Investor Day presentation (8-K EX-99.2) lists 'Montour PA' with Plant Type 'Natural Gas Peaker,' Dual-Unit, 1,508 MW, no longer describing it as coal -- and separately states Talen's gas fleet sits 'in the heart of the Marcellus shale near Leidy Hub.' (7) Talen's FY2025 Form 10-K (filed 2026-02-26) states in its own words: 'We have already completed the conversion of our Brunner Island, Montour, and H.A. Wagner plants to lower-carbon fuels' and separately describes Montour as 'A Talen-owned and operated generation facility in Washingtonville, Pennsylvania.' Three of these seven sources are Talen's own primary-source SEC disclosures (2016, 2024, 2026) and the other four are independent trade-press reporting spanning 2016-2023 -- they agree on every turning point. I could not pin an exact in-service month/day for the lateral itself (only the plant-level conversion timeline), and I could not identify the specific third-party company the 2016 8-K says would 'construct, own and operate' the pipeline, nor confirm whether that original third-party-build plan is what was actually executed or whether Talen ended up building/operating it directly -- flagging this gap honestly rather than guessing (see the Operator fill). Per this batch's explicit guidance, a 'cancelled' project found to have actually been built is a status change to operating -- exactly this case.

concerns.recommendation: correct CancelledYear from 2013 to 2017 (the year Downeast LNG, Inc. itself obtained a DOE/FE order vacating its export authority and withdrawing its pending application) and move ShelvedCancelledType from 'inferred' to 'confirmed' -- see status_reviews

(the terminal entity) and FERC never published a distinct Federal Register notice terminating Downeast Pipeline, LLC's own CP07-53 certificate docket specifically -- no FERC filing after the May-2014 final EIS was found in Federal Register full-text search on 'Downeast Pipeline'. concerns.pipeline_name: Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage System (EGTS)
concerns.recommendation: note the ~4% Capacity discrepancy against EIA's incremental-capacity figure; otherwise no change needed
concerns.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: real, independently confirmed. EIA's Natural Gas Pipeline Projects workbook carries this exact project ('Morgantown Connector Project', operator 'Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage', FERC pre-filing docket PF21-3) across every release from 2021-10 (first appearance, status 'Pre-applied', last-updated 2021-08-17) through 2026-08 (status 'Cancelled' since the 2022-01 release, last-updated 2022-01-14). A general-web search also surfaced a company fact-sheet titled 'Morgantown Connector Project' hosted at bhegts.com describing the same scope (up to 220,000 Dth/d for Monongalia County, WV customers, with 4 new compressor stations in Clinton/Centre/Franklin Counties PA and Loudoun County VA) -- consistent with the EIA record -- but that specific asset URL now 404s and has no Wayback capture (checked CDX for bhegts.com/*morgantown*: zero captures), so it is not citable; noted here as corroborating context only, not staged as a ref. CLASSIFICATION: correct -- FERC-jurisdictional interstate natural gas transmission expansion (Authority=FERC in EIA), matches the sheet's Fuel=Gas / commodity. DUPLICATE: checked against the roster's other two EGTS in-scope rows (P3169 Mid-Atlantic Chiller, P7825 Capital Area) -- EIA carries all three as separate named projects with separate dockets/scopes/counties; not the same physical facilities. NAME-COLLISION HAZARD (not a duplicate, flagging for future researchers): a completely unrelated 'Morgantown Connector' pipeline exists -- Hope Gas's ~30-mile local distribution line from Wadestown to Osage, WV, filed with the WV PSC in 2023 and placed in service ~2026 (Dominion Post / Marcellus Drilling News, May 2026 and Mar 2026) -- built by a different company (Hope Gas, a CenterPoint Energy subsidiary) for a different purpose (LDC system reliability, not FERC-jurisdictional interstate transmission) under no relationship to EGTS's cancelled PF21-3 project. Multiple search results conflated the two; confirmed via EIA's docket/operator fields and the WV PSC filing date (2023, i.e. after EGTS's project was already cancelled in Jan 2022) that they are unrelated. ATTRIBUTION: Owner1 'Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage Inc' at 100% is consistent with EGTS's own SEC 10-Q (filed 2022-09-06, CIK 1936737), which states EGTS's own stock is 100% held by its parent Eastern Energy Gas Holdings LLC (an indirect wholly-owned Berkshire Hathaway Energy subsidiary) -- i.e. EGTS is a single-entity subsidiary with no joint-venture partners, consistent with a 100% Owner1 record for its own projects; that filing does not name the Morgantown Connector project specifically, so it supports the ownership STRUCTURE claim, not a project-specific one. SPEC: Length (21 mi) and SegmentCost ($190.8M) match EIA exactly; Status/CancelledYear match (EIA shows Cancelled by the 2022-01 release, consistent with the sheet's 2022); Capacity is close but not exact -- sheet 250.00 MMcf/d vs EIA's Additional Capacity 240.00 MMcf/d, a ~4% difference that is larger than a simple rounding gap. Only one origin (EIA) has any capacity figure for this cancelled pre-filing project; searched for a second source (FERC eLibrary docket PF21-3 -- the docketsheet is a JS-rendered Angular app that returns no static content to curl/wget and the project never advanced to a public application filing, so no FERC order exists to check; Federal Register full-text search for 'Morgantown Connector' and 'PF21-3' returned zero results, consistent with a project that never left pre-filing) and found none, so this stays flagged rather than silently resolved. Recommend keeping the sheet's 250.00 unless/until a second source is found; noting EIA's 240.00 as the contested candidate.

FOUR independent sources all state the new Venice Extension pipeline segment is 36-inch, not 42-inch: (1) TETCO's original Nov 10 2021 NGA application (Federal Register notice, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/12/01/2021-26131/texas-eastern-transmission-lp-notice-of-application-and-establishing-intervention-deadline): 'a 3.0-mile, 36-inch-diameter pipeline segment ... abandon-in-place a 2.2-mile, 36-inch-diameter existing pipeline segment'; (2) FERC's Final EIS notice of availability, Feb 2023 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/02/24/2023-03836/texas-eastern-transmission-lp-notice-of-availability-of-the-final-environmental-impact-statement-for): 'an approximately 3.0-mile-long, 36-inch-diameter pipeline segment ... abandonment in place of a 2.2-mile-long, 36-inch-diameter existing pipeline segment'; (3) Enbridge's own project page (Wayback capture 2024-07-22, https://web.archive.org/web/20240722140816/https://www.enbridge.com/projects-and-infrastructure/projects/venice-extension-project): 'Construction of a 3-mile, 36-inch-diameter pipeline segment on Texas Eastern's Line 40'; (4) East Daley Analytics, reporting on the completed, in-service pipeline in Jan 2025 (https://www.eastdaley.com/media-and-news/plaquemines-lng-takes-first-gas-in-project-milestone): 'The 36-inch Venice Lateral runs three miles from TETCO's Line 40 and replaces an existing 2.2-mile segment.' All four documents describe both the OLD (abandoned) 2.2-mile segment AND the NEW 3-mile Venice Extension segment as 36-inch -- there is no design revision on the record where the new segment became 42-inch. NOTE FOR THE ORCHESTRATOR: the existing P0193 (Gator Express) shard's cross_row_leads entry states 'the NEW constructed Venice Extension segment is 42-inch,' attributed to the same East Daley 'takes first gas' article -- that reading appears to be an error (the article's actual sentence, quoted above, says 36-inch for the Venice Lateral). EIA's own dated Aug2026 release (Historical Projects (1996-2024) tab, row 1125, 'Venice Extension Project' / 'Texas Eastern Transmission', Docket CP22-15.) lists Diameter=42 for this docket in every release from 2022 onward, which is likely where GEM's current 42 originated (or a conflation with the adjacent Gator Express project, which IS 42-inch/15-mile/1,970,000 Dth/d per P0193's own sourcing) -- but EIA is one origin and is contradicted here by two FERC filings, the operator's own page, and independent trade press. concerns.recommendation: flag Capacity as a SYSTEM-level aggregate, not a segment rating, and update it to EQT's freshest disclosed figure (5,000 MMcf/d as of 2025-12-31) rather than the stale 2019-2022 figure of 4,400; the identical 4,400 MMcf/d figure is also carried on P6896 (Allegheny Valley Connector) and P6897 (Ohio Valley Connector), both individual laterals feeding INTO this system with their own much smaller true capacities
concerns.researcher_notes: ORCHESTRATOR HEADLINE FINDING. The 4,400 MMcf/d recorded for P6895 (and identically for P6896 and P6897) is Equitrans' company-wide TOTAL THROUGHPUT CAPACITY for its entire transmission-and-storage system, not a rating of any single pipe or segment. Confirmed verbatim, word-for-word, across THREE separate company disclosures spanning three years: (1) Equitrans Midstream's OVCX Exhibit Z-3 (FERC Docket CP22-, filed 2021, 'About Equitrans Midstream Corporation' boilerplate) states, for both its April 2021 non-binding notice (YE2019 data) and June 2021 binding notice (YE2020 data): 'ETRN's transmission and storage system includes approximately 950 miles of FERC-regulated interstate pipelines... total throughput capacity of approximately 4.4 Bcf per day.' (2) The company's own transmission.html investor page (Wayback capture dated 2026-01-13, content dated 'As of December 31, 2022') restates it unchanged: 'the transmission and storage system included approximately 940 miles of FERC-regulated, interstate pipelines... with total throughput capacity of approximately 4.4 Bcf per day.' So the SAME 4.4 Bcf/d (=4,400 MMcf/d) figure for the WHOLE ~940-950 mile system was disclosed unchanged from 2019 through 2022 -- explaining why it landed identically on all three GEM rows that trace to this system. (3) It has since changed: EQT Corporation's FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-02-18, post the 2024-07-22 Equitrans Midstream Merger) gives a fresh 'as of December 31, 2025' system table for the same Transmission segment: 'Pipeline miles 950 / Throughput capacity (Bcf per day) 5.0 / Interconnect points 8 / Compression units 45 / Compression horsepower 197,000' -- i.e. the true CURRENT system aggregate is now 5.0 Bcf/d (5,000 MMcf/d), not 4.4 Bcf/d. So the recorded 4,400 is both (a) a system aggregate improperly applied to what reads as a segment row, and (b) stale by roughly four years. Independent cross-check: EIA's Natural Gas Pipeline Projects dataset (May 2018 release, 'Historical Projects' sheet, Excel row 13) records the Ohio Valley Connector itself (docket CP15-41, completed 2016-10, WV->OH, 50 mi, 30/24-inch) at its OWN additional capacity of 850 MMcf/d -- an order of magnitude below 4,400 -- which independently proves at least P6897 cannot legitimately carry the system figure. All three company documents above are Equitrans/EQT-family disclosures (one origin per the tier-discipline rule), so this is staged at tier medium / independent:false despite three separate documents/years -- an independent (non-Equitrand-family) confirmation of the CURRENT 5.0 Bcf/d figure was not found this session (WebSearch budget exhausted; only SEC EDGAR, local EIA CSVs and Wayback were reachable). Recommend the orchestrator treat P6895 as the row closest to representing this system aggregate (if any of the three should retain a system-level number, it is this one), while P6896 and P6897 should be re-sourced to their own segment-specific capacities (see cross_row_leads).
