EIA's dated release history is unambiguous: the project shows status 'Announced' in every release from 2018-05 through 2021-10, then flips to 'Cancelled/On Hold' starting with the 2022-01 release (file EIA-NaturalGasPipelineProjects_Jan2022.xlsx), and its last_updated_date field is frozen at 2022-01-14 in every subsequent release through 2026-08 -- i.e. EIA has recorded no change to this project's status in 4.5+ years. Per this repo's own EIA-source convention ('the first release showing Completed or Cancelled bounds the in-service or cancellation year'), the correct CancelledYear is 2022, not 2023. (gem.wiki's own uncitable page claims a 'July 2023 EIA update' for this project, which appears to be a stale/incorrect paraphrase of the same EIA history -- not independently verified and not usable as a source regardless.) I could not find a second, non-EIA origin (news release, FERC docket withdrawal, or operator statement) confirming the cancellation -- Bark (2020) and Sightline (2019) both predate it, oilandgaswatch.org 404'd, S&P Global 403'd, and Internet Archive/Wayback returned 429s all session (concurrent-session rate limiting) so no capture could be pulled for any of those. Tier stays medium (EIA is one origin) despite high confidence in the correction.

concerns.recommendation: Corroborate or drop the 500 MMcf/d design-capacity figure; current sheet value (450) matches EIA's 'additional capacity' field but not the two secondary sources' stated design capacity.
concerns.researcher_notes: Sheet Capacity (450 MMcf/d) matches EIA's 'Additional Capacity' field exactly across all 28 releases. However, both Bark and Sightline independently and identically state the pipeline 'is designed to transport 500 million cubic feet per day with an option to double that amount in the future' -- a real, unresolved numeric conflict, not rounding. Plausible explanation (not confirmed): EIA's project_type for this row is 'Expansion' and its own documentation defines 'Additional Capacity' for an expansion as the INCREMENTAL capacity added to the broader system, not the new pipe's own full nameplate/design rating -- so 450 and 500 may describe different scopes (incremental system capacity vs. the 30-inch pipe's design capacity) rather than one of them being simply wrong. I could not reach a primary FERC docket (no docket number is on file -- EIA's docket_number field reads 'na' for this project in every release) to adjudicate definitively; WebSearch was budget-exhausted and search-engine scraping (DuckDuckGo, Bing) was unproductive this session. Left the sheet's 450 as REVERIFIED (matches EIA) and flag 500 here as the candidate/alternate figure for reviewer judgment, tier high because two independent, differently-authored sources agree exactly on 500.

concerns.recommendation: correct LengthKnownUnits from 'km' to 'mi' (the recorded magnitude 5.00 is a reasonable rounding of the true 4.8 mi in miles, not kilometers)
concerns.researcher_notes: Sheet records LengthKnown=5.00, LengthKnownUnits=km. The FERC order gives an exact figure of 4.8 total new miles (2.8 mi St. Cloud Loop + 2.0 mi Princeton Loop), and the EIA Aug2026 release (Historical Projects sheet, row 874) independently carries Miles=5 for this exact docket (CP16-472). Both sources state the figure in MILES, not kilometers -- 5.00 km would be about 3.1 mi, which matches neither source. This is a units-mislabeling defect (the magnitude '5.00' is a correct rounding of 4.8 mi, but the unit tag is wrong), not a magnitude error. Flagged as a spec caveat rather than forced into the fills[] record, which stays value-preserving per the FILL rule; recommend the unit correction be applied on review.

concerns.recommendation: correct 'Sherburned County' (typo) to 'Sherburne County'
concerns.researcher_notes: Sheet's StartPrefecture/District reads 'Sherburned County' -- a typo. The FERC order's exact phrase is 'Isanti, Sherburne, and Rice Counties, Minnesota' (no 'd'). Recommend correcting the spelling. Separately, note a schema-coverage gap rather than a GEM error: the project spans THREE counties (Isanti and Sherburne for the two pipe loops, plus Rice County for the Faribault Compressor Station addition), but the two-endpoint Start/End Location schema can only represent two of the three -- Rice County (compressor-only, no new pipe) is not capturable in this schema and is not proposed as a change, only flagged for awareness. Single-sourced to the FERC order (EIA does not carry county-level detail for this project -- its own State(s) field is the anomalous 'NM' noted above); no second source found naming the counties.

concerns.recommendation: update SegmentCost to $335,000,000 (2023) -- the recorded $75,000,000 is a stale/superseded estimate
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's SegmentCost ($75,000,000, 2023) is materially wrong for that year. EIA's own project-cost field for GTN XPress shows $75.1M ONLY in the 2021-10 and 2022-01 releases (an early FERC-application-era estimate); every release from 2022-10 through 2026-08 -- spanning the entire period from before FERC approval through project completion -- carries $335M. Two sources independent of EIA corroborate $335M for the certificated/current-era project: (1) TC PipeLines LP's original 2019-11-01 announcement already cited ~$335M for the broader program (globenewswire, WebFetch-confirmed); (2) bendbulletin.com, reporting the 2023-10-19 FERC certificate order, states 'TC Energy, proposed ... a $335 million project to increase the capacity of the pipeline.' The current [ref] cited for SegmentCost, canadianenergycentre.ca (published 2023-11-24, AFTER the FERC order and AFTER bendbulletin's $335M report), states 'the US$75 million GTN Xpress project' -- this appears to be the outdated $75.1M FERC-application-era estimate carried over in error by that article, not a genuine restatement of the approved project's cost. The recorded $75M/2023 pairing is inconsistent with every other source dated at or after the 2023 certificate order.

concerns.recommendation: correct LengthKnown from 21.60 mi to approximately 1.51 mi (sum of the three new/replaced pipe segments FERC's certificate order itemizes: a 0.80-mi extension, a 0.63-mi loop, and a 0.08-mi replacement) -- 21.6 mi does not appear anywhere in the certificate order and traces to a figure EIA has carried unchanged since the earliest Dec-2019 pre-filing snapshot, before the application (and its facilities list) even existed
concerns.researcher_notes: MAJOR SPEC DISCREPANCY. The sheet's recorded LengthKnown=21.60 mi is sourced (per EIA) to this project, but FERC's own certificate order for CP20-503 -- read and pdftotext-extracted in full (1085 lines) -- gives a complete, itemized 'Specifically, Northern proposes to:' facilities list totaling only: (1) 'an approximately 0.80-mile-long extension of its 24-inch-diameter Willmar D branch line' (Dakota/Scott Counties); (2) 'an approximately 0.63-mile-long, 24-inch-diameter pipeline loop of its Carlton interconnect branch line' (Carlton County); (3) 'replace an existing 0.08-mile-long, 8-inch-diameter branch line with a 12-inch-diameter pipeline of the same length' (Morrison County, Viking interconnect) -- 0.80+0.63+0.08 = 1.51 mi of new/replaced pipe, plus two compressor-station additions (no mileage). A grep of the full order text for every occurrence of 'mile' found only these three bullets plus one unrelated reference to Northern's system-wide '14,700-mile pipeline system' -- there is no other mileage figure anywhere in the order. Footnote 14 separately itemizes short abandoned segments (422 ft Viking branch + 10-20 ft Carlton takeoff + 140 ft Carlton CS tie-in + 60 ft Hinckley CS B-line + 150 ft Pierz CS piping = approx. 782-792 ft, approx. 0.15 mi) -- even combined with the 1.51 mi of new/replaced pipe, total facilities are nowhere close to 21.6 mi. Cross-checked against sources/eia_pipeline_projects/data/eia_projects_long.csv: the 21.6 mi figure has been CONSTANT across all 22 tracked EIA releases from 2020-01 ('Pre-applied', last_updated 2019-12-02 -- predating the July 31, 2020 application itself) straight through 2026-08 ('Completed') -- strongly suggesting 21.6 mi is either a persistent EIA data-entry artifact or traces to a broader pre-filing (PF20-1) scope never carried into the actual certificated CP20-503 project. This is a single strong primary-source origin (the FERC order) disagreeing with the sheet's existing single-origin (EIA) figure, so per the tier-discipline/disagreement rule this fill is staged at medium/independent:false despite being a direct primary-source read, rather than promoted to high. Recommend a human verify against the original PF20-1 pre-filing application exhibits (not accessed in this pass) or a post-completion as-built/compliance filing before applying the correction live.

concerns.recommendation: correct LengthKnown from 9.00 mi to 9.83 mi -- FERC's certificate order (the final, most-authoritative, post-EIS figure) states the project totals 'six segments of pipeline facilities totaling 9.83 miles'; no source consulted states 9.00 mi
concerns.researcher_notes: LENGTH DISCREPANCY across the project's own filing history, not an extraction artifact -- verified by grepping the literal mileage string in four independently pdftotext-extracted documents: the March 2022 application (Federal Register Notice of Applications, FR-2022-04-15/2022-08125): 'totaling 9.38 miles'; the August 2022 NOI to prepare an EIS (FR-2022-08-03/2022-16589): consistent per-segment breakdown; the March 2023 Final EIS notice (FR-2023-03-17/2023-05416): 'totaling 9.8 miles of pipe' (rounded); and the September 2023 certificate order, the final authorized scope (twice): 'totaling 9.83 miles'. EIA's own tracked Miles field (9.4, constant across all 16 releases 2022-10 through 2026-08) is close to but does not exactly match any of these. The sheet's currently recorded LengthKnown=9.00 mi does not match the application (9.38), the FEIS (9.8), the order (9.83), or even EIA's own carried figure (9.4) -- it is the outlier. Recommend the FERC order's 9.83 mi (the final certificated total, post-environmental-review) as the corrected value; staged at medium/independent:false since this is a single strong FERC-docket origin diverging from EIA's existing figure, per this slice's tier-discipline rule (disagreement between one strong primary source and the existing single-origin figure does not promote to high).

concerns.recommendation: correct Diameter from '8, 20, 24, 30, 36' to '4, 8, 24, 30, 36' -- the recorded '20' is the diameter of an EXISTING line (the Elk River 1st/2nd branch lines) being looped, not a new-build diameter, and the list is missing the smallest genuinely new pipe (4-inch, the Paynesville branch loop)
concerns.researcher_notes: DIAMETER DISCREPANCY sourced directly to the FERC certificate order's segment-by-segment facilities description, the single most granular source found: 'a 2.79-mile extension of the 36-inch-diameter Ventura North E-line (Segment 1); a 1.07-mile, 30-inch-diameter loop of the 20-inch-diameter Elk River 1st and 2nd branch lines (Segment 2); a 1.14-mile extension of the 24-inch-diameter Willmar D branch line (Segment 3); a 2.48-mile extension of the 8-inch-diameter Princeton tie-over loop (Segment 4); a 2.01-mile 4-inch-diameter loop of the 3-inch-diameter Paynesville branch line (Segment 5); a 0.34-mile extension of the 8-inch-diameter Tomah branch line loop (Segment 6)'. Reading this carefully: Segment 2's NEW pipe is 30-inch-diameter; the '20-inch-diameter' clause describes the EXISTING Elk River branch line being paralleled/looped, not new construction. Segment 5's NEW pipe is 4-inch-diameter (looping an existing 3-inch line). So the new-build diameter set is {36, 30, 24, 8, 4, 8} = distinct values {4, 8, 24, 30, 36} -- the sheet's recorded '20' does not belong in a new-construction diameter list, and '4' (the smallest genuinely new pipe) is missing from it. The NOI to prepare an EIS (FR-2022-08-03/2022-16589) independently corroborates the 4-inch figure: 'a 2.01-mile loop of 4-inch-diameter Paynesville Branch Line...(Paynesville 2nd Branch Line)'. Staged at medium/independent:false (single strong FERC-docket origin, the NOI corroborates but is the same FERC-docket origin per this slice's counting rule) diverging from EIA's existing figure, matching the same tier-discipline treatment used for the Length concern above.

concerns.recommendation: keep Diameter=8 as recorded; note EIA's conflicting 12in figure as likely erroneous or a different pipe segment, do not overwrite
concerns.researcher_notes: EIA's Aug2026 Natural Gas Pipeline Projects release (sheet 'Natural Gas Pipeline Projects', row 33) states Diameter=12in for this project, disagreeing with the sheet's recorded 8in. However, two independent sources describe an 8-inch, not 12-inch, line: the FAST-41 permits.performance.gov project page (Wayback capture) and Pipeline & Gas Journal's 2025-07-29 article both describe an eight-inch, low-pressure distribution-feeder-scale pipeline (consistent with Lower Valley Energy's stated purpose of replacing overland LNG trucking into the Star Valley service area with a small local supply line, not a large-diameter interstate trunk). EIA's own project notes describe it as a 'High-pressure pipeline,' which is internally inconsistent with an 8-inch NPS at typical local-distribution pressures and reads as though it may reflect a data-entry error or conflation with a different, larger project in the same docket family. Weighing 2 independent sources (permits.gov + P&GJ) describing 8in, one of them contemporaneous with actual construction, against EIA's single 12in figure: the sheet's 8in value is better corroborated. Recommending no change to the recorded Diameter, with EIA's conflicting figure flagged here rather than silently accepted; contested left as "" (evidence says EIA's own value is more likely wrong, not that the sheet's needs a specific new number).

concerns.recommendation: update LengthKnown 48.00->51.00 mi, Diameter '14, 22, 30, 36'->'30, 36' in, Capacity 150.00->144.00 MMcf/d — the sheet carries the project's original Feb-2022 PRE-FILING scope (PF22-5), not the certificated/as-built scope (CP23-15) it was actually built and completed under
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's recorded 48.0 mi / 14,22,30,36-in / 150.00 MMcf/d matches EXACTLY the EIA 'Pre-applied' record tracked under docket PF22-5 (releases Oct2022 through Jan2024, e.g. EIA-NaturalGasPipelineProjects_Jan2024.xlsx sheet 'Natural Gas Pipeline Projects' row 122: 48 mi, diameter '14, 22, 30, 36', additional_capacity 150 MMcf/d) — i.e. the sheet reflects the project as originally pre-filed in Feb 2022, before FERC certification. Once FERC issued the certificate (Dec 2023, docket CP23-15), EIA's tracking switched to the certificated scope and has read 51 mi / '30,36' in / 144 MMcf/d in every release from Apr2024 (Construction) through Aug2026 (Completed) without change — e.g. EIA-NaturalGasPipelineProjectsAug2026.xlsx sheet 'Historical Projects (1996-2024)' row 1205: miles=51, pipeline_diameter_inches='30,36', additional_capacity_mmcf_d=144, status=Completed, completed_date=2025-11-01. TC Energy's own live project page and fact sheet (both independent of EIA) corroborate the AS-BUILT numbers, not the sheet's pre-file numbers: fact sheet states 'replacing approximately 51-miles ... existing pipeline ... with larger diameter, new pipeline' and 'an incremental 144,000 dekatherms per day of natural gas capacity' (144,000 Dth/d ~ 144 MMcf/d, the same Dth/MMcf convention used elsewhere on this sheet, e.g. P2578); the live page's construction-update log itemizes the built segments as PL-1 (10.9-11 mi, 36-inch, McHenry County IL), PL-2 (16 mi, Washington/Waukesha Counties WI) and PL-3 (24 mi, Waupaca/Outagamie/Winnebago Counties WI), summing to ~51 mi. TC Energy's page independently states the 36-inch diameter for PL-1 specifically ('the replacement of 11 miles of 36-inch pipeline (PL-1) ... has been completed'); it does not itself give a diameter for PL-2/PL-3, so the '30-inch' portion of the diameter set rests on EIA alone (all EIA releases count as one origin) — noted as a partial-corroboration caveat. Two independent origins (TC Energy + EIA, both post-certification/post-completion) agree the built project is 51 mi / 144 MMcf/d, and only the 36-in diameter has full two-origin support; treat length and capacity as high tier, diameter as medium.

concerns.recommendation: Verify whether Capacity should record pipeline-only deliverability rather than the combined pipeline+storage figure currently cited.
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's Capacity (3,725 MMcf/d) is stated verbatim in its own cited source (CPUC Summer 2021 Southern California Gas Reliability Assessment, p.2), but that document is explicit that the number is NOT pipeline capacity alone: 'Pipeline and storage capacity combined can provide 3,725 million cubic feet per day (MMcfd) of natural gas' (emphasis added -- executive summary). The same document's Table 4 (Transmission Zone Assumed Operational Capacities) sums the system's three named transmission zones (Northern 870 + Wheeler Ridge 765 + Southern 670 MMcfd, plus a minor Line 85 Zone of 60 MMcfd) to roughly 2,365 MMcfd of pipeline-only inbound capacity for summer 2021 -- materially less than 3,725. So the recorded number is real and correctly quoted from its ref, but it measures a different (broader) quantity than 'pipeline capacity' as the GEM Capacity field intends. Recommend a researcher confirm the pipeline-only transmission capacity (candidate figure ~2,365 MMcfd per Table 4, though that is a single reliability-assessment snapshot, not a nameplate/certificated rating) before treating 3,725 as the pipeline's own capacity. Not overriding the value here since no single authoritative pipeline-only nameplate capacity figure was found within this pass's search budget (WebSearch quota was exhausted mid-sweep).

concerns.recommendation: Re-verify current system transmission mileage; the recorded 3,640 mi traces to a 2013 SoCalGas fact sheet (data as of Summer 2011) and may be stale.
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's LengthKnown (3,640 mi) is stated verbatim in its own cited ref (SoCalGas 'Pipeline Classifications' fact sheet, dated January 2013, citing 'Summer 2011' data: 'our 3,640-mile transmission pipeline system'). Two more recent, independently-dated documents give different, lower mileage for the same system: (1) SoCalGas's 2022 CPUC compliance filing (Rulemaking R.15-01-008, June 2022 report, Appendix 1 -- transmission-pipeline leak data by pipe material) lists two pipe-material rows for 'SoCalGas Transmission Territory' totaling 3,440 mi (1 mi 'PB' + 3,439 mi 'PC') for 2021; (2) SoCalGas's FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2026-02-26, as of 12/31/2025) states 'SoCalGas' natural gas facilities included ... 3,030 miles of transmission and storage pipelines' (note: that figure bundles transmission with storage-field piping, so it is not a clean apples-to-apples comparison to the sheet's transmission-only 3,640 mi). All three figures name the same SoCalGas system and are dated (2011-vintage, 2021-vintage, 2025-vintage respectively) but disagree by hundreds of miles, and the trend is downward over time -- consistent with either genuine retirement/consolidation of transmission mileage or a reclassification of some transmission mileage into distribution/storage categories over the intervening decade. Not proposing a replacement value here because the three sources are not measuring identical scopes (transmission-only vs. transmission+storage) and a merge-time researcher should reconcile which of the CPUC 2022 (3,440 mi, transmission-only, closest in scope to the sheet's definition) or a newer regulatory filing is the best current figure.

concerns.recommendation: check LengthKnown -- two independent, more-current sources put PG&E's backbone/local gas transmission system materially below the recorded 7,000 mi
concerns.researcher_notes: The sheet's existing ref (pge.com/gas-systems/pipeline.html) DOES state the recorded value verbatim ('PG&E's nearly 7,000 miles of gas transmission pipelines') and names the pipeline, so that unit re-verifies clean on its own terms (see the Length fill below). But casting a wider net for the required second independent source surfaced a material disagreement: (1) PHMSA's own 'PG&E System Overview' safety page states PG&E 'operates nearly 5,700 miles of gas transmission pipelines' (Wayback capture 2025-01-02); (2) PG&E Corp's 2025 Corporate Sustainability Report 'About PG&E' page states '5,650 miles of backbone and local gas transmission pipelines' (current, dated 2025); (3) PG&E Corp's FY2023 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2024, describing the system as of 2023-12-31) states 'over 6,400 miles of backbone and local transmission pipelines'. PHMSA (an independent federal regulator) and PG&E's own 2025 CSR agree within rounding at ~5,650-5,700 mi -- two independent origins pointing to a figure roughly 19-20% below the sheet's 7,000. The SEC 10-K's 6,400 (as of end-2023) sits between the two. The pge.com marketing page carrying the sheet's 7,000 figure is undated and may describe a broader definition (e.g. including some distribution-adjacent or historical mileage) or simply be stale copy. Recommend the researcher weigh 5,650-5,700 (PHMSA + 2025 CSR, the two most current, most precisely-dated, mutually-corroborating figures) against the sheet's 7,000 and update LengthKnown accordingly; candidate value given as 5650 (2025 CSR, most recent).

PEPL's own FY2021 10-K (the SEC's most recent, filed 2022-02-18) states the CURRENT system in two different ways in the same paragraph: (1) 'The Company's [Panhandle's] transmission system consists of FOUR large diameter pipelines extending approximately 1,300 miles from producing areas in the Anadarko Basin of Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas through Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and into Michigan' (i.e. a ~1,300-mile ROUTE corridor now carrying 4 parallel strings, not 1); and (2) the summary statistics table: 'Approximate Miles of Pipelines -- Panhandle 6,000' (i.e. ~6,000 total miles of PIPE when all 4 parallel strings + laterals/loops are summed -- roughly consistent with 4 x 1,300 route-miles plus loops). Wikipedia independently corroborates the larger figure: 'Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company, LP is an approximately 6,300-mile natural gas interstate pipeline system.' So there are two internally-consistent CURRENT candidates -- ~1,300 mi (route/corridor) or ~6,000-6,300 mi (total installed pipe, the figure PEPL itself reports as 'Miles of Pipelines' and that Wikipedia echoes) -- and NEITHER is 860. I propose 6,000 mi as the primary candidate because it is literally PEPL's own answer to 'how many miles of pipeline,' it is corroborated by Wikipedia's independent 6,300-mi figure, and it is the same style of system-total figure this tracker already carries on peer multi-line network rows in this same batch (P0168 CIG 6,920 mi, P0222 NGPL 9,100 mi) -- but I did not silently overwrite the cell because GEM's segment-vs-network convention for a single-row system like this one is a judgment call for a human, not a mechanical fix: if this row is meant to represent one logical route/corridor rather than total installed pipe, ~1,300 mi (also SEC-10-K-sourced) would be the better number. Either way, 860 is wrong for a currently-operating characterization of the line and should not stand uncorrected. Proposed refs (both verified, both name Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line specifically): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/76063/000007606322000010/pepl-20211231.htm and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panhandle_Eastern.

concerns.recommendation: update SegmentCost -- GEM's $2.96bn is the ORIGINAL (2009) pre-construction estimate; multiple independent sources put the actual/final project cost at roughly $3.5-3.65bn after well-documented 2010-2011 delays and overruns

All three of these independent origins (NGI's 2011 news reporting, OPB's 2011 news reporting, and the Offshore Technology project database) agree the true cost is materially above GEM's $2.96bn -- by 18-23%, well past the >=10%-of-value threshold for a material spec conflict. Both the 1926 well/local-line event and the 1929 transmission-line event are real and sourced, but NEITHER is '1920,' and the sheet gives no indication which milestone it intended. I'm flagging 1929 as the better-evidenced candidate (it is the event that produced an actual cross-border transmission pipeline named for Williston) but this deserves a closer look before pasting -- e.g. a period MDU/Montana-Dakota Utilities annual report or a state PSC record could pin it exactly. Two CPUC A.15-09-013 docket documents (SDG&E/SoCalGas's own regulatory filings, same overall proceeding but two separate data-request responses filed a year apart) state this explicitly: the 2018-03-06 DR7 response says 'The nominal capacity of Line 1600 as currently operating as part of the SDG&E transmission system is 65 MMcfd' (contrasted with proposed Line 3602 at 500 MMcfd); the 2017-09-19 SCGC-23 (DR23) response repeatedly frames 'system capacity with Line 1600 operating at 640 psig is 630 MMcfd' as the SDG&E SYSTEM total, and separately reports ACTUAL measured 2017 flows through Rainbow Metering Station into Line 1600 of only 29.96 MMcfd average / 46.32 MMcfd maximum -- an order of magnitude below 630 and consistent with the ~65 MMcfd nominal figure. This is independently corroborated by the wiki's own cited SDUT article, which says the line 'provides only about 10 percent of capacity for the San Diego area' -- 10% of the system's 630 MMcfd is ~63, matching the 65 MMcfd nominal figure almost exactly and confirming 630 was never meant to describe this segment alone. GEM's wiki page appears to have pulled '630 million cubic feet per day' from a generic EIA natural gas data portal (www.eia.gov/naturalgas/data.php) that url_verifier confirms does NOT name Line 1600 or state 630 anywhere -- a classic aggregate-figure-on-a-segment error, likely compounded by conflating the SDG&E-system figure with the segment figure. Recommend Capacity -> 65 (MMcf/d), sourced to the CPUC DR7 response; note the DR7/SCGC-23 pairing is one origin (both are SDG&E/SoCalGas's own regulatory filings in one docket), but the SDUT journalism (independent of the applicant) corroborates the ~10%-of-system proportion independently, and the actual 2017 flow data (29.96-46.32 MMcfd) is real-world telemetry that independently brackets the 65 MMcfd nominal figure from below. This is not a MISSING_VALUE fill -- the cell already carries a value, so it is staged here as a validity concern rather than a REFS_ADDED fill (the source does not agree with the sheet's 630); see the matching fills[] entry on Capacity, which is closed UNRESOLVED for the same reason and points back here.

So: FERC docket (2019 AND 2020) + the current EIA dataset + the Reuters wire on the completed project all agree on 495; nothing corroborates 450 except a superseded EIA snapshot from mid-project. Annual-update status review. The sheet records Status=cancelled/StartYear1=2022 for the whole row, sourced to a 2023 Earthjustice release about National Grid's withdrawal of the pipeline's fifth and final phase (the LNG-vaporizer connection at Greenpoint). Read in full, that same release states phases 1-4 -- the bulk of the physical 7 mi/30 in main -- were already built ('that National Grid built and profiteered from'). National Grid's own (Wayback-captured, 2022-12-27) project page independently confirms construction ran spring 2017-fall 2020 and that portions were 'placed into service prior to the 2020-2021 heating season,' and separately states the project 'is in service.' In These Times (2023-07) corroborates that the completed sections were physically connected to National Grid's existing Greenpoint facility by mid-2023 (via a smaller, older pipeline), while noting they do not distribute gas directly to households the way the cancelled vaporizer connection would have -- a genuine nuance, not a clean 'fully operating as originally designed' story. On balance the physical infrastructure GEM's row exists to track (the 7 mi/30 in main) was built and is carrying gas by 2020; recommend Status -> operating, StartYear1 -> 2020. CancelledYear=2023 remains factually accurate for the phase-5 withdrawal specifically -- see the linked spec validity concern for the vocabulary question of whether/how to retain it once Status is no longer 'cancelled'. Flagging the whole finding for orchestrator adjudication given the partial-build nuance and the schema tension, per the prompt's explicit instruction to check exactly this.

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: re-scoping the two rows as two segments (built phases 1-4 on one, cancelled phase 5 on the other). Nothing in either row's data describes phase 5 alone - both carry the FULL 7 mi / 30 in / Brownsville-Greenpoint line - and no source gives phase 5's own length or endpoints, so the split would have to be invented. The pipe is one row.
STATUS RULED: OPERATING, StartYear1=2020. This is the substantive finding of the pair, and it reverses what the sheet records on BOTH rows. National Grid's own project page states portions were 'placed into service prior to the 2020-2021 heating season' and that the project 'is in service'; the sheet's own existing Earthjustice ref, read in full, credits activists with stopping only phase 5 and describes phases 1-4 as built; In These Times (2023-07) corroborates that the completed sections were physically connected by mid-2023. What was cancelled in 2023 was the fifth phase - the LNG-vaporizer connection at Greenpoint - not the pipeline. Roughly 5.5-6 of the 7 recorded miles exist and carry gas.
CANCELLATION FIELDS RULED: CLEAR CancelledYear (2023) and ShelvedCancelledType ('confirmed') on P4070 when Status moves to operating. Both row agents correctly refused to decide this alone and escalated it. A row cannot be operating and carry a cancellation year: that pairing is exactly the defect class this slice is sweeping for, and it would misreport a built, in-service main as a cancelled project in every downstream count. The 2023 event is real and must not be lost - it is preserved in the Status ref set, in this shard's notes, and in ResearcherNotes, where a partial-scope cancellation belongs. Delayed='yes' / DelayType='confirmed' STAY: the line was proposed to run to Greenpoint and never got there.

ref_work.primary_value:
The developer of a 2 Bcf/d interstate pipeline project to transport "liquids-rich" Permian natural gas to the Louisiana Gulf Coast has requested to initiate the prefiling review process with the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and is targeting a 2028 in-service date.

DeLa Express is an affiliate of private energy infrastructure firm Moss Lake Partners. The 42-inch, 690-mile pipeline would begin in the Delaware Basin at Loving County, Texas, and supply "markets on the US Gulf Coast from Port Arthur, Texas, to Cameron Parish, Louisiana, including growing demand from liquified natural gas export facilities as well as Moss Lake's affiliated natural gas liquids export project, Hackberry NGL," it said April 2 in the prefiling request (PF24-4). It would terminate near Moss Bluff in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana.

The prefiling process would allow DeLa Express to work with stakeholders to address any environmental issues before filing its FERC certificate application, DeLa Express said. It plans to hold an open season for the pipeline and contract with shippers during the prefiling process.

DeLa Express requested FERC issue a notice approving the use of the prefiling process by April 12. Under its anticipated timeline, it would file its certificate application with FERC in February 2025, receive its FERC certificate in April 2026, begin construction in June 2026 and place the facilities into service in July 2028.

The project will include four lateral supply pipelines in the Permian and a 6.2-mile delivery lateral in Calcasieu Parish. DeLa Express also plans to build eight greenfield compressor stations along the line with 65,000 horsepower each.

Over 95% of the pipeline route is collocated with or parallel to existing utility rights of way, DeLa Express said.

CONCERN: I could not find any source stating a $121,000,000 cost for the Gulf Crossing Pipeline, and every capital-cost figure I did find for this project is roughly 10-15x higher. Boardwalk Pipeline Partners' FY2006 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2007), announcing the project, put the *combined* cost of Gulf Crossing plus its associated Gulf South/Fayetteville-Greenville expansions at 'approximately $3.3 billion' for 2007-2009. The FY2008 10-K (filed 2009) itemizes Gulf Crossing separately in its capital-projects table: 'Gulf Crossing Project -- Estimated Total Cost $1,800 [million] -- Cash Invested through December 31, 2008 $1,403.5 [million].' That is consistent with the physical scope (approximately 357 miles of new 42-inch interstate transmission pipeline plus compression, a very large-diameter, long-haul project) -- $121 million would imply roughly $340,000 per mile of 42-inch pipe including compression, which is implausibly low for a 2007-2009-vintage 42-inch interstate line (steel/labor costs were unusually high in that period, which the 10-Ks themselves flag as a cost driver). I searched SEC EDGAR full-text search for 'Gulf Crossing' plus '121' / '121,000,000' / '$121 million' and reviewed the FY2006, FY2007, FY2008, and FY2009 Boardwalk 10-Ks directly (all fetched and grepped) -- none contains a $121 million figure tied to Gulf Crossing; the closest analogous number is Boardwalk's Southeast Expansion project (a different, smaller project) at $775 million estimated cost, still far above $121 million. I also checked whether $121 million could be a partial transaction value (e.g., proceeds from Boardwalk's disclosed but apparently unconsummated plan to sell a 49% interest in Gulf Crossing to a third party) -- the 10-Ks mention that structure only in the context of the $3.3 billion aggregate figure and never state a dollar value for the 49% stake itself. ref_work.researcher_notes: This is a state-spanning multi-mainline aggregate system wholly within Texas (Waha-Katy and Waha-Carthage mainlines per the wiki description); no discrete start/end city is appropriate at the network-row grain, consistent with how other big multi-segment systems (e.g. Southern Natural Gas Pipeline) are recorded elsewhere in this tracker.

Hydrocarbons Technology (Verdict Media, trade press): 'Construction of the pipeline began in June 2010 and it became operational in December 2010.' Energy Transfer Partners LP's FY2010 Form 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2011-02-28): 'The Tiger pipeline was placed in service on December 1, 2010,' and reports transportation revenue/volumes from it through year-end 2010. A 2026-07-21 Federal Register notice (FERC Docket CP26-549-000) shows ETC Tiger Pipeline, LLC still actively operating and filing to expand capacity to serve a new gas-fired data-center power plant -- proof the line remains in service as of mid-2026, not just historically. Three distinct publishers (trade press, company SEC filing, federal register) agree the line entered and remains in service.

ETP's FY2010 10-K lists Tiger as one of its 'interstate natural gas transportation' assets, NGA-jurisdictional as a 'natural gas company.' The 2026 FERC notice describes ETC Tiger's Franklin Farms Project providing 'firm transportation capacity' of natural gas to an Entergy Louisiana gas-fired generating facility. Two distinct sources (company SEC filing; Federal Register/FERC) agree the commodity is natural gas.

The 2009 Federal Register notice records ETC Tiger's application 'pursuant to section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act' for authorization to build and operate a new interstate pipeline -- Section 7(c) certification is the definitional marker of an interstate gas transmission line. ETP's FY2010 10-K likewise lists Tiger among its NGA-jurisdictional 'interstate natural gas transportation' (transmission) assets, distinct from its intrastate gathering/processing lines. Two distinct sources (FERC/Federal Register; company SEC filing) agree it is a transmission-class interstate pipeline.

ETP's FY2010 10-K: 'In April 2010, the application to construct and operate the Tiger pipeline was approved by the FERC and field construction began on the pipeline in June 2010.' Hydrocarbons Technology: 'Construction of the pipeline began in June 2010.' Both agree exactly on June 2010 as the construction start, matching the sheet's ConstructionYear/Month (2010/6).

ETP's FY2010 10-K states plainly: 'The Tiger pipeline was placed in service on December 1, 2010.' Hydrocarbons Technology: 'it became operational in December 2010.' Both agree on a December 2010 in-service date, matching the sheet's StartYear1 (2010).

FERC's 2009 Notice of Application records ETC Tiger's request to build a pipeline 'capable of transporting up to 2,000,000 Dth/day' -- 1 Dth is essentially 1 Mcf of pipeline-quality gas, so this equals ~2,000 MMcf/d. Natural Gas Intel (2010): 'The pipeline would have the capacity to transport up to 2 Bcf/d' = 2,000 MMcf/d exactly. ETP's FY2010 10-K: 'Initial capacity of 2.0 Bcf/d.' Three distinct sources (FERC filing record, trade press, company SEC filing) agree on 2,000 MMcf/d (2 Bcf/d) initial capacity, matching the sheet exactly.

Natural Gas Intel (2010): the pipeline is 'a 175-mile, 42-inch diameter pipeline.' ETP's FY2010 10-K: 'Approximately 175 miles of interstate natural gas pipeline.' Both agree on 175 miles for the initial (as-built) line, matching the sheet's LengthKnown (175 mi) -- this is distinct from the 20-mile 2011 extension noted in later trade coverage, which is out of scope for this row's value.

Natural Gas Intel: '175-mile, 42-inch diameter pipeline.' FERC's 2009 Notice of Application: 'a new approximately 175-mile, 42-inch natural gas pipeline.' Both agree on a 42-inch diameter, matching the sheet exactly.

Hydrocarbons Technology: 'The Tiger Pipeline was laid from Catharage [sic, Carthage] in East Texas to Delhi in Louisiana... The 42in-diameter Tiger pipeline begins at the Carthage Hub... interconnects with the Houston pipeline in Panola County, East Texas. The pipeline then extends towards the east to end in Delhi, Lousiana [sic].' Energy Transfer Partners' own 2009 press release (via Wayback, the live ir.energytransfer.com URL now times out): the pipeline will 'connect to ETP's dual 42-inch pipeline system near Carthage, Texas... and end near Delhi, Louisiana.' Two distinct publishers agree on Carthage, TX as the start and Delhi, LA as the end, matching the sheet exactly.

Energy Transfer Partners LP's FY2009 Form 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2010-02-24): 'In August 2009, we filed an application for FERC authority to construct and operate the Tiger pipeline, which is pending necessary regulatory approvals. We expect the total costs of this project to be $1.2 billion, excluding the costs of the recently announced expansion.' Matches the sheet's SegmentCost (1,200,000,000 USD) exactly. Searched Natural Gas Intel, Hydrocarbons Technology (via Wayback), and the ETP FY2010 10-K (which only says the project came in 'significantly below our original cost estimates' without restating a dollar figure) for a second source repeating this $1.2 billion figure and did not find one within this session's search budget (web search quota was exhausted mid-session; only direct fetch/curl was available afterward). Single source found -> tier medium, independent false per the rule.

Hydrocarbons Technology (GlobalData), project profile: 'Construction on the project began in the first quarter of 2016 and was completed in early 2017. The pipeline came on line in March 2017.' Natural Gas Intelligence (Mar 22, 2017, cited from its seed URL, which now redirects to an unrelated current article on the live site -- confirmed via Wayback capture 2019-08-17, which passes on the full body text): 'The Trans-Pecos system is slated to come online March 31, according to a company spokeswoman.' Two distinct publishers agree the pipeline entered service in 2017 and neither source, nor any other source checked (Business Wire in-service announcement, DeSmog Blog Jan 2017, both discussed below), indicates it has since gone offline -- supports Status=operating. Live naturalgasintel.com URL 200s but silently redirects to a different, unrelated current article (the 2017 article ID no longer resolves on the live site, confirmed by curl -- a soft-redirect, not a 404), so the Wayback snapshot is proposed in its place per the blocked/moved-origin rule.

Railroad Commission of Texas Form T-4/T-4A permit application (Apr 6, 2015, Permit No. 09352; hosted on DocumentCloud, contributed by Marfa Public Radio reporter Travis Bubenik -- this IS the government document, not a navigation surface): the fluid-transported checkbox lists 'Specify Natural Gas' for the pipeline. Note the DocumentCloud VIEWER page (the seed URL) is a client-rendered shell with no server-side text -- verified its raw OCR text via the underlying asset endpoint (`assets.documentcloud.org/documents/2062745/trans-pecos-pipeline-t4-permit.txt`, same document, direct text) and propose that URL instead since it is the one that actually carries the checkable content; both resolve to the same filed document. Natural Gas Intelligence (Wayback, see Status unit) independently describes it throughout as a 'natural gas pipeline' carrying gas from the Waha Hub. Two independent origins (a Texas state regulatory filing and a trade-press article) agree.

Same RRC T-4/T-4A permit (see Fuel unit for the URL note): the permit's own cover certification reads 'INITIAL PERMIT FOR APPROXIMATELY 143 MILES OF PROPOSED 42" TO TRANSMISSION LINE', and question 3 of the application form ('Check detailed purpose(s) for which described pipeline will be used') is answered Transmission. Single explicit source for the literal word 'transmission' -- Natural Gas Intelligence and Hydrocarbons Technology both describe the pipeline as a long-haul interstate/intrastate gas line consistent with transmission service but neither uses the word itself, so kept at medium/independent=false rather than overclaiming.

CONCERN: the sources found put construction starting earlier than the sheet's September 2016. Hydrocarbons Technology's project profile states plainly: 'Construction Started Q1 2016' and 'Construction on the project began in the first quarter of 2016.' The Dallas Morning News (Jun 10, 2016), in a piece about celebrity opposition, is headlined/subtitled 'As construction starts, they're asking Dallas energy mogul Kelcy Warren to change his company's plans' -- consistent with construction already underway by June 2016, i.e. before Q3. Neither source names September 2016 specifically, and I found no source that does. Not proposing either as a ref for ConstructionYear/Month=2016-09 since both actually point to an earlier date; flagging for Update to check whether the sheet's September falls in a different phase (e.g. a specific segment or the Mexico-side/Presidio Crossing facilities, versus the main Texas intrastate line) or is a data error. Other seed citations from 2015 (Truthout May 2015, OGJ Nov 2015, Texas Monthly Sept 2015, Fronteras Apr 2015, the RRC T-4 permit itself Apr 2015) all predate any construction phase and describe permitting/eminent-domain fights, not a construction start date, so none of them bear on this unit either way.

Same two sources as Status: Hydrocarbons Technology ('completed in early 2017. The pipeline came on line in March 2017'), Natural Gas Intelligence (Mar 22, 2017 article: 'slated to come online March 31'). Grupo Carso's own 2016 Annual Report (see SegmentCost unit) independently corroborates the year with 'Start of operations: February 2017' for the Waha-Presidio project -- a third, primary owner-side source, all agreeing on 2017 (specific month varies Feb/Mar across sources -- plausibly commissioning vs. formal commercial in-service dates -- but the sheet only asserts StartYear1=2017 with no month, so this is not a conflict). Tier high/independent true off the two trade-press sources alone; Carso's report adds a third agreeing origin.

Natural Gas Intelligence: 'Trans-Pecos will have capacity to transport 1.4 Bcf/d.' Hydrocarbons Technology: 'transports approximately 1.4 billion cubic feet (bcf) of natural gas a day.' 1.4 Bcf/d = 1,400 MMcf/d, an exact match to the sheet's Capacity=1400.00 MMcf/d. Two distinct publishers agree exactly.

Hydrocarbons Technology: 'The Trans-Pecos pipeline is 148mi (238km) long.' Natural Gas Intelligence: 'the 148-mile, 42-inch diameter pipeline.' Grupo Carso's 2016 Annual Report (co-owner's own report, listing its Waha-Presidio project): 'Length of 238 kilometers and diameter of 42 inches' -- 238 km converts to 147.9 mi, matching 148 mi almost exactly. Hydrocarbons Technology: '42in in diameter.' Natural Gas Intelligence: '42-inch diameter pipeline.' RRC T-4 permit: 'PROPOSED 42" ... TRANSMISSION LINE' and the system-information worksheet lists '42" O.D.' Three independent origins (two trade press, one state regulatory filing) all agree exactly on 42 inches.

Natural Gas Intelligence: 'originates at the Waha Hub outside Fort Stockton, TX, in northern Pecos County ... terminates at the U.S.-Mexico boundary near Presidio, TX.' Hydrocarbons Technology: 'It originates in the Waha hub outside Fort Stockton in northern Pecos County ... to the US-Mexico boundary near Presidio, Texas.' RRC T-4 permit: lists the pipeline's counties as Brewster, Pecos, Presidio, TX, and a January 2015 cover letter names the specific route: 'Pipeline Name: Waha to Presido [sic], Size 42", Length 755,040 ft / 143 miles, County Pecos, Presidio, Brewster.' Three independent origins (two trade press, one state regulatory filing) agree the route runs from Fort Stockton/Waha Hub, Pecos County, TX to Presidio, TX at the Texas-Mexico border, matching StartLocation=Fort Stockton / EndLocation=Presidio exactly.

Hydrocarbons Technology: 'The $767m pipeline transports clean-burning natural gas from Pecos, Brewster and Presidio counties.' Grupo Carso's own 2016 Annual Report, in its Waha-Presidio project listing: 'Net Present Value of USD $767 million offered.' Two independent origins -- one trade press, one a co-owner's own primary financial disclosure -- agree exactly on $767 million, matching the sheet's SegmentCost=767,000,000 USD precisely.

Could not find any source stating the sheet's exact system-wide Main Line design capacity of 16,800 MMcf/d. Checked: (1) Williams' FY2025 joint 10-K (wmb-20251231.htm, CIK 99250/107263) and FY2018 10-K (wmb_20181231x10k.htm) — both describe Transco's geography and note expansion projects' incremental capacities (e.g. specific project Dth/d figures) but state no single system-wide 'Main Line' capacity number; (2) williams.com/pipeline/transco/ (fetched live, 200 OK) — its 'Operational Details' fact card gives 'System Peak Design Capacity: 19.5 million dekatherms per day' (~19,500 MMcf/d) and 'Miles of Transmission Pipeline: 10,000' and '60' compressor stations — none of these figures matches the sheet's 16,800 MMcf/d, 10,200 km, or any exact figure, and this fact card appears to describe the FULL Transco system (all laterals) rather than the 'Main Line' segment the sheet row is scoped to, so it is not proposable as a supporting match; (3) EIA's FERC-Form-61-derived 'EIA-StatetoStateCapacity_Jan2026.xlsx' workbook (Pipeline State2State Capacity tab) lists Transco's individual state-to-state border-crossing capacities for every year 1990-2025 — the single largest crossing in the most recent year (2025) is 5,118 MMcf/d (Alabama-Georgia) and no crossing or straightforward combination of crossings sums cleanly to 16,800 MMcf/d, so this dataset neither confirms nor is directly citable for a whole-system total (it measures point-to-point capacity, not a rolled-up system design capacity, and combining crossings into a system total would be original synthesis, not a citation); (4) Wikipedia's infobox gives 'discharge = 3.5 trillion cu ft per annum' (~9.59 Bcf/d average annual throughput) — a different metric (average annual throughput vs. design/peak capacity) that does not match 16,800 MMcf/d and was not proposed. FERC eLibrary (would likely hold the original certificate/expansion orders stating design capacity) is not fetchable in this environment. CONCERN: none of the company's own current materials describe a whole-system capacity anywhere near 16,800 MMcf/d as a single figure — the two figures actually found on Williams' own site (19,500 MMcf/d peak design capacity, full system) and the largest single EIA border crossing (5,118 MMcf/d) bound the true figure loosely but do not corroborate 16,800 specifically. This may reflect the sheet value being an older/point-in-time design-capacity figure for the Main Line segment specifically, which none of the sources checked isolate.

Could not find a source matching the sheet's 10,200 km (~6,340 mi) Main-Line-specific length. The two length figures found both describe the FULL Transco system (not the Main Line segment alone) and both disagree with the sheet: Wikipedia's infobox states 'length_mi = 10500' (10,500 mi = 16,900 km), and Williams' own website fact card (williams.com/pipeline/transco/) states 'Miles of Transmission Pipeline: 10,000' (10,000 mi = 16,090 km). Both whole-system figures cluster near 10,000-10,500 miles, roughly 60% longer than the sheet's 10,200 km (6,340 mi) value — consistent with a genuine scope difference (GEM's row is explicitly labelled 'SYSTEM/NETWORK INFO (Main Line)', i.e. the trunk only, excluding laterals/branches, while both found sources describe the entire system including laterals), so neither is proposed as a supporting ref for this Main-Line-specific figure (would be an orphan/non-matching ref). Checked Williams' FY2018 and FY2025 10-Ks for a Main-Line-only mileage statement — neither gives a specific mileage figure for Transco at all (narrative geographic description only). FERC eLibrary (likely holder of the original certificate documents describing Main Line-only mileage) is not fetchable in this environment. CONCERN: flagging for Update review — it is possible the sheet's 10,200 km value itself reflects a unit or scope mislabel (e.g., a Main-Line-only sub-total, or km/mi conflation, given 10,200 in miles would be 16,415 km, close to Wikipedia's 16,900 km whole-system figure) but this is speculation not confirmed by any source; not changing the value per instructions.

10-K lists it as an in-service intrastate asset (resumed service May 2018); NGI's 2022 article describes it as a live, moving-gas system up to the moment of a fire-driven shut-in (context-confirms operating status per the inferable-status rule, no evidence of permanent retirement found).
Explicitly a natural gas pipeline in every source (OGJ: 'Old Ocean natural gas pipeline'; NGI: 'natural gas transmission line').
